items.title: Hypofractionated Radiation Therapy for Localized Prostate Cancer: An ASTRO Clinical Practice Guideline
items.authors: Morgan SC, Halthore A, Jia AY, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: This guideline provides evidence-based recommendations on the use of hypofractionated external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) in patients with localized prostate cancer, including indications for moderate hypofractionation (MHF) and ultrahypofractionation (UHF), appropriate dose-fractionation regimens, target volumes, and treatment planning and delivery techniques. Methods: The American Society for Radiation Oncology convened a multidisciplinary task force to address 5 key questions related to hypofractionated EBRT in localized prostate cancer. Recommendations were based on a systematic literature review and developed using a predefined consensus-based methodology with grading of quality of evidence and strength of recommendation. Results: MHF is recommended over conventional fractionation for patients receiving EBRT across all risk groups, supported by high-quality randomized data demonstrating equivalent oncologic outcomes, toxicity, and quality of life, with shorter treatment duration that may reduce overall treatment burden. UHF is recommended as a standard treatment option for patients with low- and intermediate-risk disease electing for definitive EBRT and may be considered in selected patients with high-risk disease, preferably in the context of clinical trials. Selection of fractionation should generally be independent of patient age, comorbidity, and use of androgen deprivation therapy, although MHF may be preferred over UHF for patients with significant baseline urinary dysfunction. Evidence supports the use of contemporary image-guided, conformal treatment techniques to optimize target coverage and minimize toxicity. Guidance is also provided regarding appropriate dose-fractionation regimens, including commonly used MHF and UHF schedules, as well as target volumes and integration of pelvic nodal irradiation. Conclusions: Hypofractionated EBRT has become the predominant form of definitive radiation therapy for localized prostate cancer, supported by mature randomized evidence demonstrating comparable outcomes to conventional fractionation and reduced treatment burden. Ongoing studies will further refine patient selection, the role of UHF in higher-risk disease, and integration of advanced imaging and adaptive technologies. These evidence-based recommendations inform best clinical practices in the use of hypofractionated EBRT for localized prostate cancer.

items.title: Patient reported swallowing outcomes after prophylactic versus reactive gastrostomy during chemoradiotherapy for head and neck cancer: Results from the SwallPEG randomized trial
items.authors: Dragan T, Duprez F, Digonnet A, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To compare prophylactic (p-) versus reactive (r-) percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) placement during definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) for locally advanced, nonmetastatic head and neck carcinoma, with swallowing-related quality of life (QoL) as the primary endpoint. Materials And Methods: SwallPEG is a prospective, multicenter, randomized phase III trial of patients undergoing definitive cisplatin-based CRT. Patients were randomized 1:1 to pPEG before CRT or rPEG based on predefined nutritional criteria. All received standardized nutritional counseling, weekly dietitian assessment, and swallowing rehabilitation. The primary endpoint was swallowing-related QoL at 6 months, assessed using the MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory (MDADI) composite score. Secondary endpoints included nutritional outcomes, treatment-related toxicity, PEG-related complications, and early oncologic outcomes. Results: Fifty-seven patients were analyzed (pPEG, n = 28; rPEG, n = 29). Following a prespecified interim analysis that reached the futility boundary, the trial was closed early in the context of slow accrual. Median MDADI composite scores at 6 months were 69.5 (Q1-Q3, 60.0-80.0) and 74.7 (Q1-Q3, 58.9-87.9), respectively (P = 0.595). Swallowing function declined during CRT and subsequently recovered without a significant between-group difference. Weight loss at 6 months was comparable (-7.0 % vs - 9.0 %; P = 0.67). No significant differences were observed in treatment-related toxicity, PEG-related complications, chemotherapy delivery, or early oncologic outcomes. Conclusion: No difference in swallowing-related QoL was demonstrated between (p-) and rPEG strategies. Although interpretation is limited by early trial closure and reduced sample size, the findings support individualized PEG placement based on clinical need.

items.title: Real world clinical outcomes of deep learning based versus manual proton therapy planning for oropharyngeal cancer: A matched cohort study
items.authors: van Bruggen IG, van der Laan HP, Hessels AC, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Recent deep learning (DL)-based planning approaches to intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) have shown promise for improving planning efficiency and quality. A recent study demonstrated clinical acceptable DL-based plan quality in patients with oropharyngeal cancer (OPC), this study used real-world clinical outcomes to compare oncological outcomes acute and early late side effects between OPC patients treated with DL-based IMPT and those treated with manual planning. Methods: In this observational matched cohort study, OPC patients were treated with DL-based IMPT, and were matched 1:1 to a recent manually planned IMPT cohort (74 vs 74). In DL-based planning, U-Net predicted dose distributions were robustly optimized and manually refined for approximately two hours. Overall survival, progression-free survival, locoregional control, and distant metastasis-free survival were evaluated using survival analysis. Acute and early late side effects were prospectively assessed according to CTCAE v4.0 and patient-rated symptoms were scored using the EORTC QLQH&N35 questionnaire at baseline, weekly during treatment, 12 weeks, 6 months and 12 months after treatment start. The impact of the planning method was evaluated using generalized estimating equations adjusted for baseline values. Results: No statistically significant differences were observed for any oncological outcome. Similarly, no statistically significant differences in acute and early late side effects were observed between DL-based and manual planning. Conclusion: In real-world clinical practice, the findings of this study provide no evidence that DL-based IMPT is associated with different oncological outcomes or side effects than manual planning. These findings support the clinical implementation of DL-based planning in patients with OPC.

items.title: Model-Based Normal Tissue Complication Probability Comparison Between Proton and Photon Therapies for Brain Tumors Complying With Planning Study Guidelines
items.authors: Higaki H, Nishioka K, Yokokawa K, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: The benefit of proton beam therapy (PBT) for primary brain tumors compared with x-ray therapy has not been demonstrated by randomized controlled trials. We performed a model-based approach study to evaluate the potential benefit of PBT for brain tumors using the normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models complying with the Radiotherapy Treatment plannINg study Guidelines (RATING). Methods And Materials: Sixty-six patients with primary brain tumors treated with PBT were registered. We used 11 NTCP models, calculated NTCP for each adverse event, and estimated the PBT and intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) plans for the entire patient population and for groups classified by pathology. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed for statistically significant differences between the 2 modalities, and a 2-tailed test was considered significant when <.05. A reduction was considered clinically meaningful when the difference in NTCP between the 2 modalities (ΔNTCP) exceeded the prespecified threshold. Results: Overall, PBT reduced NTCP from the cataracts, delayed recall, memory impairment, contralateral hearing impairment, and tinnitus. Patients with meningiomas and low-grade gliomas had similar tendencies. PBT was associated with a lower excess absolute risk of secondary cancer of the central nervous system in all patients. However, NTCPs for alopecia, blindness, and brain necrosis were higher in the PBT cohort, highlighting important clinical trade-offs. Thirty-one patients (47.0%) had at least 1 ΔNTCP above the specified threshold. Conclusions: In this model-based planning comparison, PBT was associated with lower estimated NTCPs for selected endpoints compared with virtual IMRT, whereas IMRT showed advantages for alopecia, blindness, and brain necrosis. PBT may offer meaningful clinical benefits, particularly in reducing the excess absolute risk of secondary cancer for patients with long-term survival. In addition, the comparison based on Radiotherapy Treatment plannINg study Guidelines made the study more objective than similar previous studies.

items.title: Radiation therapy quality assurance (RT QA) of adjuvant fractionated radiotherapy for WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma in the ROAM/EORTC1308 trial
items.authors: Mayles HMO, Haylock BJ, Whitfield G, et al.
items.abstract: Introduction: ROAM/EORTC-1308 is an international (Europe and Australasia) phase III randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing radiotherapy (60Gy/30#) to observation after surgery for WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma. The treatment plans of all the patients randomised to radiotherapy were reviewed and approved prior to treatment delivery. Pretrial credentialling included outlining and planning a benchmark case. Materials And Methods: Variations from the guidelines were noted in QA reports both for the Benchmark Case (BM) and for on-trial Individual Case Reviews (ICRs). After the trial, the QA reports were used to analyse the variations in the BM and ICRs. A random 10% of the ICRs were reviewed again independently. In all cases the reviewer agreed with the original decision. Results: 58 centres opened, of which 56 centres (20 UK, 25 EORTC, 11 TROG) submitted BM. Two centres did not undergo radiotherapy credentialling and closed without recruiting any patients. Resubmissions were: 4 (7%) for outlining and 11 (20%) for planning. During the trial 66 patients at 28 centres received radiotherapy, (median 2 patients per site). Resubmissions for ICRs were: 31 (48%) sets of outlines (3 cases twice) and 12 (18%) treatment plans (1 plan twice). There were 28 instances of major variations in the ICR outlines and 14 in the ICR plans. Conclusions: For complex radiotherapy of uncommon tumours, a pre-trial QA is insufficient and prospective ICRs of all patients are required. The consistent high-quality radiotherapy in ROAM/EORTC1308 ensures the primary outcome is robust and that there was no variation in radiotherapy treatment across sites.

items.title: KEYNOTE-867: A Phase III, Randomized, Double-Blind Study of Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy With Pembrolizumab for Unresected Stage I or II Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
items.authors: Jabbour SK, Sótér S, Eaton M, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is standard of care for inoperable stage I or II non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). KEYNOTE-867 (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03924869) evaluated the addition of pembrolizumab to SBRT in participants diagnosed with stage I or II NSCLC that was inoperable or in participants who refused surgery. Methods: Adults with untreated, stage I or II (T1 to limited T3, N0, M0) NSCLC (AJCC 8th edition) that was inoperable, or adults who refused surgery, were randomly assigned 1:1 to thoracic SBRT to primary tumors for ≤2 weeks concomitantly with pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo once every 3 weeks for ≤17 cycles. The primary end point was event-free survival (EFS) by blinded independent central review. Results: A total of 448 participants were randomly assigned to SBRT plus pembrolizumab (n = 227) or SBRT plus placebo (n = 221). The median time from random assignment to the data cutoff date (June 11, 2024) for the prespecified first interim analysis was 20.6 (range, 1.3-56.8) months. The median EFS (95% CI) was 31.2 (22.5 to 39.1) months and 28.3 (19.8 to 33.1) months for the pembrolizumab and placebo arms, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.69 to 1.24]; P = .2932). Among participants who received ≥1 dose of study treatment, grade 3-5 treatment-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in 46/226 (20.4%) participants in the pembrolizumab arm and 8/218 (3.7%) participants in the placebo arm. There were five treatment-related deaths all of which occurred in the pembrolizumab arm (2.2%). Conclusion: The addition of pembrolizumab to SBRT did not improve EFS and was associated with a higher incidence of treatment-related AEs compared with SBRT alone in participants with inoperable stage I or II NSCLC. Based on the benefit-risk profile, the KEYNOTE-867 trial was prematurely stopped, and all study treatment was discontinued.

items.title: Combining locoregional treatments and immunotherapies in patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma
items.authors: Cioni D, Mauro E, Feng D, et al.
items.abstract: The systemic treatment landscape of unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma has been transformed by immune-checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based regimens. These advances have led to efforts to combine ICIs with locoregional therapies (LRTs), particularly transarterial chemoembolization, transarterial radioembolization and external beam radiotherapy, in an attempt to improve tumour control and extend the benefits of ICIs to patients with intermediate-stage disease. The rationale for this combination approach is provided by the ability of LRTs to induce immunogenic cell death and tumour antigen release and to reprogramme the immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment. Five phase III trials have thus far shown improvements in progression-free survival and objective response rates with regimens combining ICIs with transarterial chemoembolization. Early-phase and real-world data also support the combination of ICIs with transarterial radioembolization or external beam radiotherapy, particularly in selected patients with focal disease unsuitable for embolization or portal vein tumour thrombosis. However, various challenges remain, including patient selection and therapy sequencing, response assessment, and the growing difficulties in demonstrating survival advantages in the context of widespread post-progression crossover and effective subsequent therapies. In this Review, we describe the biological rationale, summarize the clinical evidence and discuss future directions for trial design, imaging and biomarker-driven patient selection in the integration of LRTs with immune-based regimens for patients with unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma.

items.title: Omission of Radiation Therapy is Associated with Inferior Disease Control in High Risk Early-Stage Hodgkin Lymphoma
items.authors: Dave NK, Dreyfuss AD, Moskowitz AJ, et al.
items.abstract: Early-stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is highly curable, yet optimal frontline treatment remains contested. Combined modality therapy (CMT) with chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy (RT) has been the standard, but concern over RT-associated toxicities has driven adoption of chemotherapy-alone approaches despite randomized trials failing to demonstrate noninferiority with RT omission. We analyzed 810 adult patients treated across eight academic centers for stage I/II HL between 1/2012 and 1/2022, comparing outcomes with CMT and chemotherapy alone. Primary endpoints were progression-free (PFS) and overall survival (OS); propensity-score matching was conducted to homogenize baseline characteristics between the groups, and subgroup analyses were conducted to identify clinical features associated with differential benefit. Among 480 propensity-matched patients, five-year OS was 98.6% with CMT versus 97.3% with chemotherapy alone (p=0.620); five-year PFS was 87.2% vs 81.4% (p=0.053). CMT conferred significantly superior PFS in patients with bulky disease (91.8% vs 73.0%; HR 3.77; p=0.005) and interim (iPET)-positive disease (Deauville score (DS)≥4; 74.9% vs 51.9%; HR 2.97; p=0.020). iPET response was the strongest independent predictor of both progression (HR 7.02) and mortality (HR 6.97), with PFS declining markedly across DS groups (DS1-2: 92.2%; DS3: 79.4%; DS4-5: 46.4%). Among iPET-positive patients, those receiving unplanned consolidative RT required less salvage therapy than those managed with chemotherapy escalation alone (29.0% vs. 45.2%; p=0.037). Late toxicities were more frequent with CMT, though 69% of second malignancies occurred outside the RT field. These findings support risk-adapted, biomarker-driven treatment selection and the need for prospective trials incorporating modern RT techniques and iPET-adapted algorithms.

items.title: Three-fraction preoperative stereotactic radiotherapy for resectable brain metastases: the phase 2 STEP trial
items.authors: Biau J, Thillays F, Le Fèvre C, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Postoperative stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) is the standard adjuvant treatment after resection of brain metastases. It nevertheless requires delineation of a dynamic postsurgical cavity, delays local treatment by 3 to 6 weeks (and thus resumption of systemic therapy) and carries substantial risks of radiation necrosis and leptomeningeal disease. Preoperative SRT targets an intact lesion and may address some of these limitations. Methods In this open-label, single-arm, multicenter phase 2 trial, eligible adults had a Karnofsky performance status ≥70 and up to four brain metastases, including one resectable lesion ≤5 cm, from breast, non–small cell lung, kidney, or digestive cancer or melanoma. Patients received preoperative SRT (three fractions of 7.7 Gy prescribed to the encompassing 70% isodose line, equivalent to 11Gy per fraction at the isocenter) followed by surgical resection within 3 days of the last fraction. The primary outcome was 6-month local control on centrally reviewed MRI. Secondary outcomes included index-lesion radiation necrosis, leptomeningeal disease, distant intracranial control, overall survival, toxicity, cognition, and quality of life. Results Of 73 patients assessed, 67 were eligible and 63 received both SRT and surgery. Median age was 62 years. At a median follow-up of 12.7 months, the 6-month local control rate was 100% (95% CI, 95%–100%), meeting the primary endpoint; the 12-month rate was 96.4% (95% CI, 87%–99%). No leptomeningeal disease occurred. The 1-year cumulative incidence of index-lesion radiation necrosis was 7% (95% CI, 2%–16%), meeting the key secondary endpoint. Distant intracranial failure occurred in 22 patients (35%); 12-month overall survival was 81.2% (95% CI, 70%–89%). Postoperative complications occurred in 4 patients (6.3%); cognition and quality of life remained stable over the 12 months of protocol follow-up. Conclusions Three-fraction preoperative SRT followed by resection was associated with high local control, low radiation necrosis, and no leptomeningeal disease, supporting evaluation in ongoing randomized trials.

items.title: JS6-2 Total neoadjuvant therapy for rectal cancer: current status and future directions
items.authors: Y. Kagawa, J. Watanabe, K. Ando, H. Bando, T. Hashimoto, R. Suwa, T. Kato, K. Oba, E. Oki, T. Yoshino
items.abstract: Total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) has reshaped the management of locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) by prioritizing distant control, treatment completion, and the possibility of organ preservation. Phase III trials (RAPIDO, PRODIGE 23, STELLAR) consistently demonstrate higher pathological complete response rates and reductions in distant failure with TNT compared with conventional long-course chemoradiotherapy strategies, translating into improved disease-related outcomes and, in PRODIGE 23, overall survival benefits.

items.title: Preliminary evaluation of ProSpare(®), a rectal obturator for prostate bed radiotherapy within the randomised multicentre POPS trial (NCT02978014)
items.authors: Stewart S, Thomas K, Parmar J, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: The introduction of volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) has enabled dosimetric improvements during prostate bed (PB) radiotherapy; however, the planning target volume (PTV) margins remain substantially greater than for prostate radiotherapy. New approaches are required to further optimise rectal dose and minimise target and organ motion. ProSpare®, a self-inserted rectal obturator designed to facilitate daily image guidance, may enhance radiotherapy accuracy and reduce treatment-related morbidity. Materials And Methods: Patients scheduled to receive adjuvant or salvage PB radiotherapy after radical prostatectomy were randomised to either standard-of-care (SOC) PB-IMRT using centre-standard PTV margins and verification protocol (SOC) or PB-IMRT with daily ProSpare®-guided radiotherapy using a reduced 5-mm posterior margin. Dose and fractionation schedules were selected by each centre according to protocol recommendations. The primary endpoint is patient-reported EPIC bowel function and bother at 2 years. Secondary endpoints include acute Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) and CTCAE toxicity, patient-reported outcomes, device tolerability, and anorectal dosimetry. We report the results from the prespecified analysis of these secondary endpoints. Results: Between 2017 and 2023, 162 patients were recruited; 158 began radiotherapy and were evaluable at 18 weeks. Acute toxicity data were available for 146 patients (SOC 76/81, ProSpare 70/77). Compared with SOC, ProSpare® was associated with lower 18-week RTOG ≥grade 1 gastrointestinal (GI) and genitourinary (GU) toxicity (39% vs. 31% and 37% vs. 29%, respectively). The incidence of worst CTCAE grade 2 GI and GU toxicity was <6%. Of 51 responders, 50 found ProSpare® tolerable and would recommend its use. Use of ProSpare® resulted in consistently lower ano-rectal dose-volume parameters. Conclusion: ProSpare®-guided prostate bed radiotherapy (PBRT) resulted in lower acute RTOG bowel toxicity at all time points. Patient-reported tolerability was very favourable. Use of ProSpare® improved rectal and anal canal dosimetry. Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, identifier NCT02978014.

items.title: Stereotactic body radiotherapy for oligometastatic ovarian cancer: Current evidence, patient selection, and future directions
items.authors: Lucia F, Deiana L, Dupré PF, et al.
items.abstract: Ovarian cancer recurs in a limited number of sites in a significant proportion of patients, raising interest in metastasis-directed therapy to delay systemic treatment escalation. Stereotactic body radiotherapy is increasingly used in this context. This review synthesises the available evidence on the role of stereotactic body radiotherapy in oligometastatic ovarian cancer, with emphasis on prospective data, patient selection criteria, integration with systemic therapies, and emerging technological approaches. The phase II trial MITO-RT3/RAD, first prospective, multicentre study in this setting reported excellent results in terms of complete response rates and local control at 12 months, with complete response emerging as a strong predictor of local control. The treatment was also very well tolerated, with no grade3 or worse toxicity and a low rate of grade 1-2 toxicity. Stereotactic body radiotherapy is a safe, effective metastasis-directed therapy option endorsed by current European guidelines. Key unresolved questions include the optimal integration with poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors, the surgery versus stereotactic body radiotherapy comparison, and the management of peritoneal oligometastatic disease. The randomised ENGOT-ov74/LoRiO trial will address several of these gaps.

items.title: PARP Inhibitors in the Management of Ovarian Cancer: ASCO Living Guideline, Version 2026.1.0
items.authors: Tew WP, Lacchetti C, Adams TS, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: This living guideline provides recommendations on the use of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPis) in the management of epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC). Methods: An Expert Panel developed recommendations based on a systematic review of randomized controlled trials, and cohort studies evaluating homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) testing and PARPi efficacy and safety. Results: The updated evidence base comprises 79 publications, including 18 studies evaluating 13 homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) assays and 31 pivotal trials assessing PARPi efficacy and safety. Frontline trials demonstrated progression-free survival benefits. However, later-line treatment and recurrent maintenance trials reported potential overall survival disadvantages. Recommendations: All patients with newly diagnosed advanced EOC should undergo genetic testing, and HRD tumor testing if BRCA-negative, using FDA-approved or prospectively validated companion diagnostic assays. In advanced EOC, PARPi maintenance should be prioritized for the first clinical remission. Frontline PARPi monotherapy maintenance should be offered after platinum-based chemotherapy response to patients with germline or somatic BRCA1/2 mutations or HRD-positive disease. Olaparib plus bevacizumab maintenance may be offered to patients responding to first-line platinum-based chemotherapy plus bevacizumab who have BRCA1/2 mutations or HRD-positive disease. PARPi maintenance therapy is not recommended for patients with non-BRCAmut HRD-negative tumors or early-stage EOC. In the recurrent setting, PARPi maintenance should be restricted primarily to PARPi-naïve patients with BRCA1/2 mutations responding to second-line or greater platinum-based chemotherapy. Monotherapy PARPi should not be offered for the treatment of recurrent EOC outside clinical trials. Furthermore, PARPi are not recommended for use in combination with chemotherapy, other targeted agents, or immune-oncology agents outside a clinical trial. Clinicians should monitor for serious adverse events, including myelodysplastic syndrome, acute myeloid leukemia, and pulmonary complications.

items.title: Chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy as adjuvant treatment for head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma: a meta-analysis
items.authors: Young TC, Yap WK, Chang KP, et al.
items.abstract: Objectives: The benefit of adding chemotherapy to postoperative radiotherapy for head and neck adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) remains uncertain. We compared adjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CRT) with radiotherapy (RT) alone. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception through May 6, 2026, with manual reference-list checking. Comparative studies reporting time-to-event outcomes for CRT versus RT were eligible. Hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and the Hartung-Knapp adjustment. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261485857). Results: Eight studies contributed 836 outcome-specific observations. CRT was not associated with improved overall survival (six studies; 648 patients; HR, 0.99; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.70-1.41; I2 = 0%), disease-free/progression-free survival (five studies; 534 patients; HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.81-1.34; I2 = 0%), or distant metastasis-free survival (six studies; 574 patients; HR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.55-1.63; I2 = 44.5%). Neither locoregional control (two studies; 354 patients; HR, 0.09; 95% CI, 0.00-59.00) nor locoregional failure-free survival (three studies; 262 patients; HR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.32-2.60) improved significantly; both estimates were imprecise. Results were consistent in adjusted-versus-unadjusted subgroup and leave-one-out analyses. Conclusion: Available nonrandomized evidence does not demonstrate that adjuvant CRT improves survival compared with RT alone in head and neck ACC. Evidence for locoregional outcomes remains sparse and imprecise. These findings do not support routine chemotherapy but favor individualized treatment decisions.

items.title: Darovasertib and Crizotinib First-Line Treatment for Metastatic Uveal Melanoma: Overall Survival, Efficacy, and Safety From the OptimUM-01 Study
items.authors: McKean M, Chmielowski B, Butler MO, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Metastatic uveal melanoma (mUM) has poor prognosis with limited therapies. GNAQ/11 mutations that activate protein kinase C (PKC) are detected in 95% of UM tumors. Darovasertib is a first-in-class, oral, targeted PKC inhibitor that, in combination with the MET inhibitor crizotinib, has shown responses and encouraging survival outcomes in early mUM clinical trials. Here, we present phase 2 results in first-line patients with mUM treated with darovasertib 300 mg twice a day and crizotinib 200 mg twice a day. Methods: The OptimUM-01 study was a phase I/II, multicenter, open-label, dose escalation and expansion study of darovasertib in patients with solid tumors harboring GNAQ/11 mutations irrespective of human leukocyte antigen status; this analysis focuses on the phase II expansion in previously untreated patients with mUM. Eligibility criteria included Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1 measurable disease, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-1, and adequate organ function. Study end points included safety, objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DOR), disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). Results: Overall, 44 treatment-naïve patients were enrolled. The most common adverse events (AEs) were diarrhea (95.2%), nausea (84.1%), peripheral edema (61.4%), and vomiting (52.3%). The most common grade 3 or greater AEs were pulmonary embolism (9.1%) and iron deficiency anemia (6.8%). AEs leading to discontinuation occurred in three patients (6.8%). ORR was 34.1%, DOR was 9.0 months, and DCR was 90.2% at 8 weeks. The median PFS and OS were 7.0 months (95% CI, 5.0 to 8.3) and 21.1 months (95% CI, 11.9 to 20.7), respectively. Conclusion: Results from OptimUM-01 suggest that the combination of darovasertib and crizotinib has encouraging efficacy with a manageable safety profile and may represent a first-in-class targeted treatment option for patients with previously untreated mUM.

items.authors: David Collingridge
items.abstract: TQB2102, a novel HER2 bispecific antibody–drug conjugate (ADC), combined with bemotrizumab and capecitabine shows promising anti-tumour activity in patients with gastric or gastroesophageal junction (GC/GEJ) cancer and will be assessed in a future phase 3 trial, according to Miaozhen Qiu (Guangzhou, China) on behalf of a multicentred trials group in China. Presenting results from a phase 2 trial, Qiu described outcomes for 86 patients with HER2+ GC/GEJ cancer who had been assigned to three different cohorts: high-dose ADC plus bemotrizumab, high-dose ADC plus bemotrizumab and capecitabine, or low-dose ADC plus bemotrizumab and capecitabine.

items.title: Benmelstobart With or Without Anlotinib After Chemoradiotherapy for Unresectable Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: The R-ALPS Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Ji Y, Li Q, Chen L, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Consolidation immunotherapy improves outcomes after chemoradiotherapy for unresectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Disease progression remains common, and more effective consolidation strategies are needed. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of benmelstobart with or without anlotinib as consolidation therapy after chemoradiotherapy for unresectable stage III NSCLC. Design, Setting, And Participants: This multicenter double-blind phase 3 randomized clinical trial took place at 42 centers in China from 2020 to 2023 among patients with unresectable stage III NSCLC without progression after concurrent or sequential chemoradiotherapy. In stage 1, patients were randomized 1:1:1 to 2 active regimens or placebo; in stage 2, additional patients were randomized 1:1 between the active regimens to power their direct comparison. Data cutoffs were November 30, 2023, for stage 1 and July 8, 2024, for the pooled analysis. Data analysis was performed from January 17 to March 23, 2025. Interventions: Patients were randomized to receive benmelstobart plus anlotinib, benmelstobart plus anlotinib placebo, or their matching placebos. Main Outcomes And Measures: Primary end point was independent review committee (IRC)-assessed progression-free survival (PFS). Results: Of 553 participants (median [IQR] age, 62 [56-67] years; 495 male individuals [89.5%]), 390 were randomized in stage 1 and 163 in stage 2. In stage 1, median PFS was 15.1 months (95% CI, 9.4-21.7) with benmelstobart plus anlotinib, 9.7 months (95% CI, 6.0-34.4) with benmelstobart alone, and 4.2 months (95% CI, 3.2-6.8) with placebo. The hazard ratios (HRs) were 0.49 (95% CI, 0.36-0.66; P < .001) for benmelstobart plus anlotinib vs placebo and 0.53 (95% CI, 0.39-0.72; P < .001) for benmelstobart vs placebo. In the pooled stage 1 and 2 analysis, median PFS was 17.4 (95% CI, 12.5-24.8) months with benmelstobart plus anlotinib and 11.2 (95% CI, 7.0-20.7) months with benmelstobart alone (HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.63-1.08; P = .12). Grade 3 to 5 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 48.8%, 29.4%, and 19.7% in the benmelstobart plus anlotinib, benmelstobart alone, and placebo groups, respectively; grade 5 events occurred in 7.2%, 1.4%, and 1.5%, respectively. Conclusions And Relevance: This randomized clinical trial found that benmelstobart with or without anlotinib significantly improved PFS compared with placebo. Adding anlotinib did not significantly improve PFS compared with benmelstobart alone and increased severe and fatal treatment-related adverse events.…

items.title: Meeting the Need: Development of a Theranostics-Focused Nuclear Oncology Physics Fellowship
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Walter YA, Wu HT, Lokitz S, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose/Objectives: With the emergence of radiotheranostics, radiation oncology practices are adapting to offer new radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs), while qualified medical physicists (QMPs) support these programs. However, RPT-specific medical physics training is variable, and heavily dependent on the clinical setting. QMPs may therefore be tasked with supporting RPT programs without adequate training in the subject matter. In 2025, the Nuclear Oncology Division of the Department of Radiation Oncology at Willis Knighton Cancer Center launched a first-of-kind, one-year Nuclear Oncology Physics Fellowship. Here, we detail our program structure and provide a framework for further expansion of nuclear oncology medical physics training. Methods: The fellowship is offered in partnership with three institutions: a large, tertiary community cancer center (hub site), a radiopharmaceutical research institution encompassing GMP isotope and radiopharmaceutical production and clinical and pre-clinical imaging, and a medical physics consulting group. The curriculum is split into twelve rotations covering the core competencies outlined by major certifying bodies. Primary mentors hold board certifications in diagnostic, nuclear medicine, or therapeutic medical physics. Results: The fellowship may be completed before or after physics residency training, and culminates in a final project, in which the trainee designs a mock theranostics department. The program was verified to meet current training requirements for board certification in nuclear medicine physics. At the time of writing, the program enrolled its first fellow (pre-residency) and recruited its second trainee (post-residency). Conclusion: The fellowship provides a pathway for QMPs to gain the necessary training to support new theranostics programs. The curriculum may be adapted to accommodate the interests of each trainee and extended to support individuals in other crucial professions within the theranostics space. Future development of RPT-specific training guidelines may influence adjustments to the curriculum and certification processes; however, the current model provides a robust template for necessary QMP training.

items.title: Implementing Image-Guided Brachytherapy (IGBT) For Cervical Cancer in Resource-Limited Settings: An International Multicentric Cross-Sectional Study of Resource and Workflow Impact
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Hande V, Ndarukwa S, Rubio AP, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Use of image-guided brachytherapy (IGBT) in cervical cancer improves patient outcomes. However, implementation in resource-limited settings is challenging due to limited capacity upscale, absence of workflow enhancement strategies, and financial barriers. Optimizing workflows is essential, yet the relationship between workflow efficiency and IGBT uptake remains unclear. Methods: This cross-sectional study examined brachytherapy (BT) workflows across 14 nationally representative centers. Standardized forms collected data on infrastructure, treatment workflows ((A): Conventional two-dimensional (2D) X-Ray-Guided BT, with point-A-based fractions planned using 2D X-ray imaging, (B): Standard intracavitary (IC) three-dimensional (3D) IGBT, with fractions planned using computed tomography (CT)- or magnetic resonance (MR)-based imaging with volume-based prescriptions, (C): Advanced 3D IGBT, with fractions delivered using advanced IC or intracavitary-interstitial (IC-IS) techniques and planned using CT- or MR-based imaging with volume-based prescriptions.)), procedural times, anesthesia, imaging, and treatment planning. National BT resource data was also collected. Recommendations were developed to optimize workflows and facilitate IGBT transition. Findings: A total of 365 workflows were analyzed, wherein workflow B was most common (51%). Median procedure times were 2 hours 08 minutes (Interquartile range (IQR) 1 hour and 7 minutes), 2 hours 35 minutes (IQR 1 hour and 51 minutes), and 4 hours 16 minutes (IQR 2 hours and 33 minutes) for workflows A, B, and C, respectively. Using sedation instead of full anesthesia shortened workflows by a median of 35 minutes. BT machine demand, based on national cervical cancer incidence, ranged from 0.2 to 9.5; four countries had low (< 0.5), two moderate (0.5 - 1.0), and eight high demand (>1.0). Resource- and context-specific recommendations for IGBT transition were provided. Interpretation: BT workflows varied widely. Substantially increased procedure times and resource use were observed with advanced workflows. Findings highlight opportunities to improve efficiency through anesthesia choice, imaging strategy, and planning workflow optimization. Implementing context-specific strategies will be crucial for IGBT transition. Funding: Funding from the XXXX, in collaboration with XXXX and participating sites.

items.title: Curative-intent management of de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma: an evidence-based consensus guideline from the International Collaborating Oncology Organisations
items.authors: Guo QJ, Liu Q, Bossi P, et al.
items.abstract: Patients with de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma were historically deemed incurable and treated with palliative intent. Emergence of potent systemic therapy in combination with local treatment for both locoregional and metastatic diseases has enabled long-term survival in some patients. This international guideline was developed through consensus-building by 54 experts from 46 centres across 18 countries or regions and endorsed by 17 oncology organisations. 32 recommendations across seven clinical domains were formulated, including 29 strong (≥80% agreement [consensus] or high quality of evidence) and three conditional recommendations (67-79% agreement). We recommend that curative-intent treatment should be offered to medically fit patients with no more than three metastatic lesions in two or fewer organs at baseline or following response to systemic therapy; multimodality treatment (comprising immunochemotherapy, locoregional radiotherapy, metastasis-directed therapy, and maintenance therapy) is recommended. This guideline provides a practical framework for standardisation of clinical management of de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma and identification of key evidence gaps for future research.

items.title: Intensity-modulated radiotherapy combined with albumin-bound paclitaxel and platinum-based chemotherapy for locoregional recurrent cervical cancer: a single-institutional phase II investigator-initiated nonrandomized clinical trial
items.authors: Fang C, Liu S, Xia J, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: To prospectively explore efficacy and safety of radiotherapy combined with albumin-bound paclitaxel and platinum-based chemotherapy for locoregional recurrent cervical cancer (CC). Methods: Patients with locoregional recurrent CC were enrolled in the analysis. The enrolled patients received radiotherapy and albumin-bound paclitaxel and platinum-based chemotherapy. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS). Secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rate (ORR), and safety. Results: 99 patients were enrolled. For all patients, the 3-year PFS and 3-year OS were 48.5% and 58.6%. 17.2% of patients achieved CR and 67.7% of patients achieved PR. The ORR was 84.8%. Moreover, 10.1% of patients were confirmed SD. The DCR was 94.9%. Conclusion: Locoregional recurrent CC could benefit from radiotherapy combined with albumin-bound paclitaxel and platinum-based chemotherapy.

items.title: Limosilactobacillus reuteri for oral mucositis in patients undergoing radiotherapy for malignant head and neck tumors: a randomized controlled trial
items.authors: Gao K, Li YT, Pei YY, et al.
items.abstract: Oral mucositis (OM) is a major toxicity in patients with head and neck cancer undergoing radiotherapy. Here we conducted a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized phase II trial (NCT06285591) from March 2024 to January 2025 at West China Hospital of Sichuan University to evaluate whether Limosilactobacillus reuteri (L. reuteri) supplementation could reduce severe OM (SOM; WHO Oral Toxicity criteria grade ≥3). A total of 160 patients were randomly assigned to receive L. reuteri probiotic lozenges or placebo twice daily during radiotherapy. The primary endpoint was the incidence of SOM, and secondary endpoints included SOM onset and duration, as well as the incidence, onset, and duration of any-grade OM. Safety outcomes were monitored throughout the study. The primary endpoint was met, with a lower incidence of SOM in the L. reuteri group than in the placebo group (37.5% vs 61.3%; relative risk 0.61; 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.85; absolute risk reduction 23.8 percentage points, 95% CI 8.7% to 38.8%; P = 0.004). L. reuteri supplementation also delayed SOM onset and shortened SOM duration. No significant safety concerns were observed. These findings indicate that L. reuteri supplementation reduces SOM incidence and severity in patients with head and neck cancer receiving radiotherapy.

items.title: Organ Preservation With Watch and Wait in Patients With Rectal Cancer
items.authors: Keeling SS, Behman R, Hu CY, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: With growing evidence and evolving guidelines, organ preservation with watch and wait for stage II to III rectal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy is increasingly implemented. However, the true frequency of watch-and-wait use is unknown. Objective: To estimate rates of intentional organ preservation with watch and wait by evaluating secular trends across age groups. Design, Setting, And Participants: This retrospective cohort study used data from the National Cancer Database (NCDB), with analyses conducted in September 2025. Patients with stage II to III rectal cancer diagnosed between 2006 and 2023 who received neoadjuvant chemoradiation in Commission on Cancer-accredited hospitals participating in the NCDB across the US were included. Exposure: Age, year of diagnosis, and treatment strategy (proctectomy vs nonsurgical management). Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome consisted of watch-and-wait rates, defined as excess nonsurgical management greater than baseline. To account for nonsurgical management unrelated to the decision for watch and wait, joinpoint regression estimated baseline rates of nonsurgical management and annual percentage changes. A secondary analysis examined associations of age and year with watch-and-wait rates using multivariable logistic regression. Results: Among 101 001 patients with rectal cancer (median [IQR] age, 60 [51-69] years; 37 957 female [37.58%]), 84 324 underwent surgery and 16 677 did not. Baseline rates of nonsurgical management remained stable through 2014. Joinpoints occurred in 2014 and 2019, with annual percentage changes of -0.45% (95% CI, -2.26% to 0.78%; P = .42) in 2006 to 2014, 9.83% (95% CI, 4.66% to 13.73%; P = .001) in 2015 to 2018, and 21.71% (95% CI, 17.74% to 29.57%; P < .001) in 2019 to 2023. Baseline nonsurgical management increased with age, from 1331 of 19 785 patients younger than 50 years (6.73%) to 1748 of 6210 patients aged 80 years and older (28.15%). Earlier adoption occurred in older patients; the group aged 80 years and older surpassed 5-percentage point excess watch and wait by 2015 (33.78% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [5.63-percentage point excess]) and 10% by 2017 (39.56% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [11.41-percentage point excess]), compared with 2019 (12.88% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [6.15-percentage point excess]) and 2021 (20.75% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [14.02%] excess) in patients younger than 50 years. Overall, watch and wait increased from 140 of 6101 patients (2.30%) in 2015 to 2068 of 6280 patients (32.94%) in 2023.…

items.title: Exercise Training During Neoadjuvant Treatment for Gastroesophageal Cancer and Tumor Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Simonsen C, de Heer P, Thomsen SN, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Physical deterioration and disease progression during neoadjuvant treatment can preclude tumor surgery in patients with gastroesophageal cancer. Whether preoperative exercise training can increase the probability of undergoing tumor surgery remains unknown. Objective: To compare exercise training with usual care on the likelihood of not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent after neoadjuvant treatment for gastroesophageal cancer. Design, Setting, And Participants: PRESET-RCT was a single-blinded, parallel-group, 2-arm, superiority randomized clinical trial. Patients with gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma scheduled to undergo treatment with curative intent, including neoadjuvant treatment, and with no contraindication to exercise training were eligible. Participants were enrolled at University Hospital Copenhagen, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, Denmark, from August 16, 2018, to September 23, 2022, with final follow-up on October 22, 2024. Data analysis was performed from March 2023 to May 2025. Intervention: The participants were randomized 1:1 to preoperative exercise training from diagnosis until tumor surgery or control. The intervention consisted of twice-weekly concurrent aerobic exercise and resistance training. Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent. The secondary outcomes were treatment tolerance and overall survival. Results: In total, 207 participants (73.7%) were randomized and 202 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analyses (mean [SD] age, 65.3 [8.5] years; 161 [78.9%] male; 170 [83.3%] with gastroesophageal junction cancer), with 101 randomized to each group. In the exercise group, 10 (9.9%) did not undergo tumor surgery with curative intent compared with 8 (7.9%) in the control group (odds ratio, 1.28; 95% CI, 0.48-3.38; P = .62). There were no between-group differences in permanent discontinuation of neoadjuvant treatment (odds ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.38-1.72) or postoperative complications (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.61-2.20). The overall survival rates at 3 years for the exercise and control group were 51.0% and 65.0%, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.02-2.45). Conclusion And Relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, preoperative exercise training did not increase the likelihood of undergoing tumor surgery for patients with gastroesophageal cancer.…

items.title: Extended follow-up of tarlatamab in patients with small-cell lung cancer after platinum-based chemotherapy in the randomized phase III DeLLphi-304 study
items.authors: Rudin CM, Ahn MJ, Schuler M, et al.
items.abstract: Background: In the DeLLphi-304 trial, at a median follow-up of <12 months, tarlatamab significantly improved overall survival (OS; P < 0.001), progression-free survival (PFS; P = 0.002), and patient-reported outcomes (PROs), and demonstrated a favorable safety profile versus chemotherapy. We report efficacy and safety outcomes after extended follow-up in patients with small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). Patients And Methods: In this phase III, open-label trial, patients with SCLC whose disease had progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy were randomly assigned (1 : 1) to receive either tarlatamab or chemotherapy (topotecan, lurbinectedin, or amrubicin) until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or death. The primary endpoint was OS. Secondary endpoints included investigator-assessed PFS, objective response, disease control, duration of response per RECIST v1.1, PROs, and safety. Results: As of data cut-off (18 February 2026), median OS was 13.6 and 8.4 months with tarlatamab and chemotherapy, respectively (median follow-up, 23.3 and 22.8 months). Median PFS was 4.2 and 3.2 months, respectively (median follow-up, 22.2 and 21.9 months). Kaplan-Meier estimated OS rates at 12 and 24 months were 55.9% and 30.3% with tarlatamab versus 39% and 14.9% with chemotherapy; corresponding PFS rates at 12 and 24 months were 20.6% and 14.2% versus 5.9% and 2.3%. Objective response rate was 35.4% with tarlatamab, including six confirmed complete responses versus 20.4% with chemotherapy; at data cut-off, ongoing responses were observed in 31.1% (28 of 90) versus 3.8% (2 of 52) of responders, respectively. Sustained disease control for ≥52 weeks was observed in 24.4% versus 4.3%. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) led to treatment discontinuation in 3.2% versus 6.6%; grade ≥3 events decreased over time, with no serious TRAEs with onset ≥12 months. Cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome occurred early in treatment and were predominantly low grade. Conclusions: With extended follow-up, tarlatamab continues to demonstrate sustained and durable clinical benefit and a favorable long-term tolerability profile versus chemotherapy, in patients with SCLC after first-line platinum-based chemotherapy, supporting its use as the standard of care in this setting.

items.title: Postoperative radiotherapy after radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer: Patient selection, target delineation and contemporary evidence
items.authors: Huck C, Zobouyan C, Pignot G, et al.
items.abstract: Following radical cystectomy, muscle-invasive bladder cancer remains associated with a substantial risk of locoregional recurrence, particularly in patients with pT3-4 disease, nodal involvement, positive surgical margins, or limited pelvic lymph node dissection. Historically, adjuvant radiotherapy reduced pelvic recurrence rates but was largely abandoned because of toxicity concerns associated with older radiation techniques. The development of intensity-modulated radiotherapy, image-guided radiotherapy, contemporary contouring guidelines, and modern dose constraints has renewed interest in adjuvant radiotherapy. Recent randomized trials, including Bladder-ART/GETUG-AFU30 and BART, have demonstrated that modern adjuvant radiotherapy can be safely delivered and significantly improve locoregional control in selected high-risk patients. Current International Bladder Investigator Society recommendations have standardized target volume delineation, including pelvic nodal regions and cystectomy bed. At the same time, the management of muscle-invasive bladder cancer is rapidly evolving with the integration of immune checkpoint inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates and circulating tumor DNA-guided based treatment strategies. Future research should focus on refining patient selection and integrating adjuvant radiotherapy within a personalized multimodal approach combining clinicopathological risk factors, molecular biomarkers, and contemporary systemic therapies.

items.title: Neoadjuvant Therapy in Patients with Upper Tract Urothelial Cancer: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.authors: Di Bello F, Gallioli A, D'Andrea D, et al.
items.abstract: Context: The role of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) in patients with upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) remains controversial, mainly because of the lack of high-level evidence. Objective: We aim to update the evidence on NAC regarding pathological and oncological outcomes in patients with nonmetastatic UTUC. Moreover, we also aimed to give an overview of neoadjuvant immunotherapy (NAI) in the current clinical scenario. Evidence Acquisition: A systematic review of 41 studies on NAC and NAI (eight prospective studies [PS] or randomized clinical trials [RCTs] and 33 retrospective studies [RS]) was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. Outcomes of interest included pathological complete response (pCR), pathological partial response (pPR), pathological downstaging, overall survival (OS), cancer-specific survival (CSS), and disease-free survival (DFS). Pooled analyses were performed using effect sizes for pathological outcomes and hazard ratios (HRs) for survival outcomes. Finally, 5-yr proportions were summarized when a 5-yr time threshold was available. Evidence Synthesis: Of the 41 articles, 30 (five PS or RCTs and 25 RS) were eligible for meta-analysis (n = 2384 patients). The pooled pCR, pPR, and pathological downstaging rates were, respectively, 11% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 10-12), 44% (95% CI: 38-50), and 20% (95% CI: 10-37). Compared with radical nephroureterectomy (RNU), NAC was associated with pooled HRs of 0.56 (95% CI: 0.39-0.80) for OS, 0.47 (95% CI: 0.26-0.85) for CSS, and 0.55 (95% CI: 0.24-1.26) for DFS. Evidence on NAI remains limited in terms of sample size and is primarily derived from early-phase studies. Conclusions: NAC was associated with favorable oncological outcomes compared with RNU alone. Nevertheless, the absence of prospective randomized studies limits the strength of the evidence, and further high-quality trials are warranted to confirm these findings.

items.title: CERVICAL CANCER: NATIONAL CLINICAL PRACTICE GUIDELINES FROM THE FRENCH CERVICAL CANCER GUIDELINES GROUP
items.authors: Carcopino X, Ouldamer L, Huchon C, et al.
items.abstract: Over the past decade, cervical cancer management has evolved substantially, with major changes in surgical approach, surgical radicality, nodal staging, imaging, radiotherapy techniques, brachytherapy and systemic treatments. To harmonize practice and integrate new evidence into clinically applicable recommendations, the French Cervical Cancer Guidelines Group developed national clinical practice guidelines for the management of patients with cervical cancer. The guideline process was conducted under the auspices of the French National College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and involved a multidisciplinary expert panel representing the French scientific societies involved in cervical cancer care. Clinical questions were formulated using the PICO framework and addressed the full continuum of care, including initial assessment, imaging, diagnostic conization, surgical nodal staging, treatment, fertility preservation, response assessment, follow-up, recurrence and specific clinical situations. Evidence was reviewed and critically appraised according to the GRADE methodology, and all recommendations were based on the 2018 FIGO staging system. External validation was performed through a two-round Delphi process involving 87 independent reviewers. Overall, 130 PICO questions generated 158 recommendations, including 35 strong and 52 weak recommendations, while no recommendation could be issued for 71 questions. Key practice-changing recommendations include the role of diagnostic conization in early-stage assessment, avoidance of minimally invasive hysterectomy from stage IB1 disease, risk-adapted surgical radicality, sentinel lymph node biopsy with ultrastaging, image-guided brachytherapy after chemoradiotherapy, and integration of PEMBROLIZUMAB in selected locally advanced or metastatic settings.

items.title: Problematic control arms in National Cancer Institute myeloma trials
items.authors: Jacqueline Kunesh, Ghulam Rehman Mohyuddin
items.abstract: Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41571-026-01221-3 Three of five National Cancer Institute-sponsored randomized trials that are currently enrolling patients with multiple myeloma have control arms that no longer reflect the standard of care, despite two of these trials being activated in 2026. Comparators in federally sponsored trials need reassessment and, if necessary, updating to reflect changes in clinical practice before and during enrolment.

items.title: Treatment Outcomes in Osteosarcoma of the Head and Neck: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.authors: Magri A, Quaiattini A, Mlynarek A, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Head and neck osteosarcomas (HNOS) are rare, accounting for ~1% of head and neck malignancies. This study systematically evaluated the role of chemotherapy (CT) and radiotherapy (RT) on survival outcomes. Methods A systematic review and meta‐analysis were performed following PRISMA guidelines across six databases. Treatment arms included surgery alone or combined with CT and/or RT, given in neoadjuvant or adjuvant settings. Primary outcomes were overall survival (OS) and disease‐free survival (DFS). Results Thirty‐one studies comprising 2006 patients were included. Jaw tumors had superior OS compared to skull base tumors. CT significantly improved OS (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62–0.89) and DFS (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63–0.98), particularly in the neoadjuvant setting, whereas RT showed no survival benefit. Conclusions Systemic therapy in combination with surgery improves OS and DFS in HNOS, reinforcing its importance as part of curative‐intent treatment.

items.title: [Radiotherapy of head and neck cancer : Highlights from the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting]
items.authors: Schnellhardt S, Tribius S, Linxweiler M, et al.
items.abstract: At the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting, several studies focused on radiotherapy of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). The phase III AREST trial showed that adjuvant radiotherapy for early oral cavity cancer with intermediate-risk features can reduce the risk of locoregional recurrence. A post hoc analysis of the JCOG1008 trial found no increased locoregional recurrence rate even when adjuvant chemoradiotherapy was initiated later than recommended. Combined radioimmunotherapy (RIT) was also a major topic this year: in a subgroup analysis of the NIVOPOSTOP trial, the disease-free survival (DFS) benefit of nivolumab was maintained in patients with extensive neck dissection, which weakens the frequently highlighted mechanistic relevance of regional lymph nodes for the immune response. In the treatment of human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive oropharyngeal cancer, results for RIT were conflicting: the phase II CCTG HN.9 trial evaluating radiotherapy combined with durvalumab failed to meet its efficacy endpoint, whereas the phase II KEYCHAIN trial of definitive RIT with pembrolizumab demonstrated a significant improvement in progression-free survival (PFS) compared with cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy. In addition, a subgroup analysis of the combined positive score (CPS) ≥ 10 population of the KEYNOTE-412 trial underscored the importance of biomarker-based patient selection when combining radiotherapy and immunotherapy.

items.title: Efficacy and Safety of Short-Course Radiotherapy Alone or Combined With Consolidation Chemotherapy Versus Conventional Long-Course Chemoradiotherapy for Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.authors: Wang C, Han Y, Xue S, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Short-course radiotherapy (SCRT)-based regimens, including SCRT-alone and SCRT-based total neoadjuvant therapy (SCRT-based TNT, defined as SCRT followed by consolidation chemotherapy), have emerged as alternative neoadjuvant options to long-course chemoradiotherapy (LCCRT) for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). This meta-analysis stratified analyses by the type of SCRT regimen and whether LCCRT arms received preoperative consolidation chemotherapy, to systematically compare their efficacy and safety and inform personalized treatment selection. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing SCRT-based regimens and LCCRT up to November 2025. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Pooled analyses were conducted using Review Manager 5.3, with relative risk (RR) or hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: Nine randomized trials (reported in 16 publications), involving 3,061 patients, were included. In the primary comparison of SCRT-based TNT versus standard LCCRT, the SCRT-based TNT group achieved a significantly higher pathological complete response rate (RR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.24-1.97, P = 0.0002), whereas tumor downstaging and locoregional failure showed no significant differences from the LCCRT group. The SCRT-based TNT regimen was associated with a significantly higher incidence of grade ≥ 3 acute toxicity (RR = 1.63, 95% CI: 1.14-2.34, P = 0.008), and showed numerical trends toward improved overall survival (HR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.76-1.28, P = 0.91) and disease-free survival (HR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.77-1.43, P = 0.77) that did not reach statistical significance. SCRT alone was associated with lower pCR (RR = 0.13, 95% CI: 0.03-0.51, P = 0.003) and downstaging rates (RR = 0.66, 95% CI: 0.56-0.79, P < 0.00001) but a markedly lower incidence of acute toxicity (RR = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.05-0.29, P < 0.00001). An exploratory analysis based on a single small trial found no significant differences between SCRT-based TNT and LCCRT-based TNT across all major endpoints. Pooling all SCRT-based strategies obscured clinically meaningful heterogeneity and yielded no significant differences for any primary endpoint. Conclusions: SCRT-based TNT significantly improves pCR compared with standard LCCRT but does not translate into survival benefit, with a numerical increase in locoregional failure.…

items.title: Surgical Margin and Risk of Local Recurrence in Children and Young Adults With Nonrhabdomyosarcoma Soft Tissue Sarcoma: A Nonrandomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Hiniker SM, Dixon AH, Xue W, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: The extent of negative margin necessary to achieve a high rate of local tumor control in children and young adult patients with nonrhabdomyosarcoma soft tissue sarcomas (NRSTS) is unknown. Objective: To evaluate the impact of negative margin extent on local tumor control in children and young adult patients with NRSTS undergoing R0 resection as part of risk-adapted multimodality treatment. Design, Setting, And Participants: This multicenter prospective clinical trial was conducted at Children's Oncology Group (COG) member sites from February 2007 through February 2012. Analysis was performed on the final dataset June 30, 2018, with a median follow-up of 6.2 years. Reviewers of margin status/extent were blinded to local control outcomes. Patients included 266 eligible/evaluable individuals younger than 30 years with nonmetastatic NRSTS who were enrolled in the COG ARST0332 trial and underwent upfront or delayed R0 resection as part of treatment. Patients who underwent an amputation or did not receive protocol-specified radiotherapy were excluded. These data were analyzed from January 2023 through July 2026. Intervention: Risk-adapted treatment included 3 patient groups with upfront or delayed surgery with or without radiation therapy with or without ifosfamide/doxorubicin chemotherapy, based on the extent of initial resection, surgical margin status, tumor size, and histologic grade. Main Outcomes: Cumulative incidence of local recurrence based on treatment approach and surgical margin extent and outcomes after local recurrence. Results: Of 266 patients (median age 13.7 [range, 2.1-27.6] years; 138 female [52%] and 128 male [48%]) who underwent upfront (n = 207) or delayed (n = 59) R0 resection, 132 had measured surgical margins: 1 mm (n = 56), 2 to 5 mm (n = 50), or 6-mm or larger (n = 26). The 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence overall was 4.4%. Local recurrence occurred in 10 of 178 patients treated with surgery alone (5.6%) and 2 of 88 patients treated with surgery and chemoradiotherapy (2.3%). Among the 132 patients with measured surgical margins, the 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence was 4.9% for 1-mm margins, 2.0% for 2- to 5-mm margins, and 0% for 6-mm or larger margins.…

items.title: 5-year outcomes of chemotherapy de-escalation in HER2-positive early breast cancer and exploratory circulating tumor DNA analyses from the randomized phase 2 PHERGain trial
items.authors: Pérez-García JM, Cortés J, Ruiz-Borrego M, et al.
items.abstract: PHERGain was a randomized, non-comparative phase 2 trial evaluating a positron 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (18F-FDG-PET)-guided, pathological complete response (pCR)-adapted strategy to omit chemotherapy in HER2-positive early breast cancer. Female patients with HER2-positive stages I-IIIA operable breast cancer (tumor size ≥ 1.5 cm) were randomized to receive chemotherapy plus trastuzumab and pertuzumab (HP; group A) or HP ± endocrine therapy (group B). In group B, treatment was adapted according to 18F-FDG-PET response after two cycles and pCR, with chemotherapy administered to nonresponders or patients without pCR. We previously reported that this de-escalation approach revealed a 3-year invasive disease-free survival (iDFS) of 94.3% (95% confidence interval (CI): 90.9 to 96.8) in group B. Here we report the prespecified secondary endpoint, 5-year iDFS and exploratory circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) findings. After a median follow-up of 5.6 years, the 5-year iDFS was 89.5% (95% CI: 85.7 to 93.4) in group B (n = 267) and 92.4% (95% CI: 86.7 to 98.5) among 18F-FDG-PET responders achieving pCR without chemotherapy (n = 86), with one distant recurrence. The latter estimate describes a long-term outcome in a post-randomization subgroup defined by 18F-FDG-PET response and pCR and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as causal effects of omitting chemotherapy. Detectable ctDNA at baseline or during treatment was associated with inferior iDFS, whereas ctDNA clearance correlated with higher pCR rates and improved long-term outcomes. These findings continue to support the clinical validity of an 18F-FDG-PET-guided, pCR-adapted approach and suggest a potential role for ctDNA in refining treatment individualization. items.title: Impact of psychosocial interventions on cancer survival: an updated meta-analysis
items.authors: McCarvell V, McCurdy-Franks E, Caini S, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Psychosocial interventions are known to improve emotional well-being and quality of life in patients with cancer, but their effects on overall survival (OS) remain unclear. An updated meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was performed. Methods A systematic literature search was performed in MEDLINE, EMBASE and Cochrane CENTRAL from database inception until December 2025. Randomized controlled trials comparing OS between patients receiving psychosocial interventions and control groups were included. Study characteristics and summary hazard ratios (SHR) were extracted. If SHRs were not provided, they were derived from Kaplan-Meier curves. A meta-analysis was performed using a random effects model. Results Of 20365 studies identified, 24 RCTs involving 4795 patients met inclusion criteria. Follow-up time ranged from 1 to 18 years. Patients treated with psychosocial interventions had better overall survival outcomes than those in the control groups (SHR = 0.87, 95% CI 0.77–0.99; I² = 45%). Subgroup analyses showed improved OS among studies involving patients treated with curative intent (12 studies; SHR 0.75, 95% CI 0.64–0.87; I² = 20.9%), studies involving colorectal primary cancers (2 studies; SHR 0.69, 95% CI 0.48–0.99; I² = 0%), and intervention duration ≥ 12 months (N = 13, SHR = 0.85, CI: 0.72-0.99, I2 = 46.8%). Conclusions Adult patients with cancer who were offered psychosocial interventions may have improved OS. Given the moderate heterogeneity in our analysis, an individual patient-level meta-analysis may help identify characteristics of patients who benefit from these interventions.

items.title: A prospective randomized evaluation of AI assisted GTV contouring in head-and-neck radiotherapy
items.authors: Rasmussen ME, Ren J, Nijkamp JA, et al.
items.abstract: Background: AI-assisted contouring has demonstrated efficiency and consistency benefits for organs-at-risk in radiotherapy. However, its impact on gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation remains unexplored. The aim of this study was to evaluate AI-assisted GTV contouring in head and neck cancer radiotherapy in an exploratory randomized controlled clinical trial. Methods: In this prospective, single-centre, randomized controlled evaluation, patients referred for curative-intent radiotherapy of head-neck cancer were randomized to manual contouring (control) or AI-assisted contouring (intervention) of gross tumor volumes using an in-house developed segmentation model. The primary endpoint was the extent of editing during a blinded multidisciplinary target conference, using normalized Added Path Length (APL). Secondary endpoints included conference duration, self-reported contouring time, and perceived complexity of the cases. Results: Between Sept 11, 2023, and Jan 20, 2025, 85 patients were enrolled; 83 were included in the analysis (41 control, 42 AI-assisted). The median difference in APL (AI-assisted minus control, negative favoring the intervention) was -0.02 [-0.32; 0.07] for GTV-T and 0.06 [-0.01; 0.14] for GTV-N. Conference duration, contouring time, and perceived complexity were similar between groups. No adverse events were reported. Conclusion: The median difference in APL between groups was consistent with no relevant effect for GTV-T. For GTV-N, however, AI-assisted contouring tended towards more editing during peer review for APL, but not for supplementary contour metrics. No efficiency benefits were demonstrated. Overall, these findings do not indicate a concern, but warrants further research before widespread adoption.

items.title: A multicenter, prospective, phase 2 trial on proton re-irradiation for patients with previously treated head and neck cancer
items.authors: Dee EC, Barker CA, Kalman NS, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Re‐irradiation (re‐RT) for recurrent head and neck cancer (HNC) can be potentially curative but is constrained by significant toxicity. Proton therapy may improve the therapeutic ratio. This multicenter phase 2 trial evaluated the safety and efficacy of proton re‐RT in patients with HNC. Methods Patients received prior HNC radiotherapy at a dose of ≥40 gray (Gy). Salvage surgery and/or systemic therapy before re‐RT were permitted. Considering clinical status, two pragmatic treatment approaches were used: fractionated re‐RT (F‐Re‐RT; 60–70 Gy) or QUAD shot re‐RT (QS‐Re‐RT; 14.8 Gy per cycle, up to four cycles; maximum total, 59.2 Gy). Primary end points were locoregional recurrence–free rates at 12 months for F‐Re‐RT and at 6 months for QS‐Re‐RT, and a fixed‐time, binary proportion analyzed using 90% Clopper–Pearson confidence intervals (CIs) and prespecified success thresholds (lower bound, >55% and >10%, respectively). Secondary end points included overall survival (OS), progression‐free survival, the cumulative incidence of distant metastasis and locoregional recurrence, clinician‐reported toxicity, and patient‐reported outcomes. Results From July 2017 to November 2022, 85 patients received either F‐Re‐RT (n = 57) or QS‐Re‐RT (n = 28), with a median follow‐up of 38 months. The locoregional recurrence–free rates were 71% (90% CI, 59%–81%) at 12 months for F‐Re‐RT and 76% (90% CI, 58%–89%) at 6 months for QS‐Re‐RT, surpassing prespecified success thresholds. The highest late toxicity attributable to re‐RT was grade 3 in 20% of patients, grade 4 in 11%, and grade 5 in 4%. The 5‐year OS rate was 29%, and the 5‐year progression‐free survival rate was 23%. Patient‐reported outcomes were stable at 1 year after F‐Re‐RT and after QS‐Re‐RT. Conclusions Proton re‐RT demonstrated encouraging locoregional control and survival in heavily pretreated patients, although late toxicities remain important concerns (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03217188).

items.title: Zamtocabtagene autoleucel, a tandem CD20-CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy, for second line treatment of large B-cell lymphoma in patients ineligible for transplantation (DALY 2-EU): primary analysis of an open-label, multicentre, randomised phase 2 study
items.authors: Borchmann P, van Meerten T, Iacoboni G, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy is the standard second-line treatment for patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. However, there is no evidence from randomised controlled trials in patients ineligible for transplantation. To address this gap, we compared zamtocabtagene autoleucel (zamto-cel), a CAR T-cell therapy directed at CD20 and CD19, with rituximab-gemcitabine-oxaliplatin (R-GemOx) chemoimmunotherapy in patients ineligible for transplantation with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma. Methods: DALY 2-EU is an open-label, multicentre, randomised, phase 2 trial conducted at 45 centres across 12 countries in Europe. Eligible patients were adults (aged ≥18 years) with second-line relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma confirmed histologically who were ineligible for transplantation and had received first-line chemoimmunotherapy containing a combination of an anthracycline-based regimen and an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of 2 or less. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to zamto-cel (single intravenous infusion of 2·5 × 106 fresh (ie, non-cryopreserved) CAR T-cells per kg, capped at 100 kg, produced in a closed automated system) or R-GemOx (rituximab [375 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1], gemcitabine [1000 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1 or 2], and oxaliplatin [100 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1 or 2] administered for up to eight 14-day cycles). Randomisation was done with an interactive web response system and stratified by age, gender, lactate dehydrogenase, International Prognostic Index, histology, time to relapse after the start of first-line therapy, and country. The primary endpoint was event-free survival assessed by a masked independent review committee and compared all patients randomly assigned to the zamto-cel and R-GemOx groups using a one-sided log-rank test. Safety was assessed in all patients who received study treatment. This ongoing trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04844866). Findings: Between Oct 14, 2021, and Jul 16, 2024, 219 patients were screened and 160 were randomly assigned to zamto-cel (n=82) and R-GemOx (n=78). The median age was 74·0 years (IQR 70·5-77·0). Patients were predominantly male (100 [63%] of 160 were men and 60 [38%] women) and White (91 [57%]), with race not reported for 64 (40%). items.title: Survival After Risk-Reducing Mastectomy in Patients With Pathogenic Variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2: A Network Meta-Analysis
items.authors: Beshar I, Viveros-Carreño D, Agusti N, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: The independent survival benefit of risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM), separate from risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO), remains uncertain among patients with pathogenic variants (PVs) in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. Objective: To evaluate the association of RRM, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based screening, and mammography alone with all-cause and breast cancer-specific mortality using RRSO-adjusted estimates. Data Sources: MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 1990, to May 28, 2026. Search structures, subject headings, and keywords were tailored to each database. Study Selection: Inclusion criteria were English-language prospective and retrospective observational studies of adult female patients with PV or likely PV in BRCA1 and BRCA2 who underwent RRM or breast cancer screening (MRI-based with or without mammography, or mammography alone), with RRSO excluded by design or adjusted for in multivariable analysis. Studies including females with prior breast or ovarian cancer were excluded. Data Extraction And Synthesis: Study reporting followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 network meta-analysis extension. Two authors independently performed study selection, data extraction, and bias assessment using a risk-of-bias assessment tool (ROBINS-I V2) and a grading approach (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation [GRADE]). Frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was performed with surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) estimation. Sensitivity analysis was conducted for the BRCA1 cohort. Main Outcomes And Measures: Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcome was breast cancer-specific mortality. All outcomes were analyzed and reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with corresponding 95% CIs. Results: Five observational studies with 7937 female patients (median [range] age, 35.9 [unreported] years to 43.4 [32.0-55.7] years) met the inclusion criteria. RRM was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with MRI-based screening (HR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.63) and mammography alone (HR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.08-0.32). RRM was also associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality compared with mammography alone (HR, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.44) but did not have significantly lower mortality than MRI-based screening (HR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.05-1.35).…
