items.title: Laparoscopic Versus Open Liver Resection for Colorectal Liver Metastases : An Individual Participant Data Meta-analysis of Four Randomized Clinical Trials
items.authors: Olij B, Pilz da Cunha G, Pugh SA, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have compared laparoscopic liver resection (LLR) and open liver resection (OLR) for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM); however, long-term outcomes and subgroup effects have not been comprehensively evaluated. Purpose: To compare postoperative and long-term oncologic outcomes after LLR versus OLR for CRLM using individual participant data from RCTs. Data Sources: PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched from database inception through March 2025 for RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM. Study Selection: Eligible studies were RCTs comparing LLR and OLR for CRLM. Data Extraction: Individual participant data, including unpublished data, were obtained from trial investigators of all 4 published RCTs. Data Synthesis: Analyses used a modified intention-to-treat approach and 1-stage individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA) with trial-adjusted regression models and g-computation to estimate standardized treatment effects across outcomes, with 95% CIs obtained by nonparametric bootstrap resampling. Prespecified subgroup analyses assessed heterogeneity of treatment effect for the primary outcome. A total of 761 patients were included (laparoscopic, n = 384; open, n = 377). Postoperative morbidity was lower in patients assigned to laparoscopic surgery compared with open surgery (19% vs. 27%). Among patients who received preoperative systemic therapy, morbidity did not differ between groups (25% vs. 24%). Ninety-day mortality was 1.8% after LLR and 0.8% after OLR. After a median follow-up of 93 months, overall survival and disease-free survival did not differ between groups. Limitation: Analyses were limited to variables available across all studies. Conclusion: In this IPDMA of all published RCTs in the field, LLR for CRLM was associated with lower postoperative morbidity than OLR, with similar long-term oncologic outcomes. Primary Funding Source: None. (PROSPERO: CRD42024502655).

items.title: Global greenhouse gas emissions from external beam radiotherapy: a population-based study
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Zhu H, Meattini I, Zhang L, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To assess the global and country-level greenhouse gas emissions implications of external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) scale-up to 2050. Methods And Materials: We conducted a country-level, scenario-based study across 181 countries to estimate EBRT-associated greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 and project emissions to 2050 under utilisation benchmarks of 50% and 64%, uniform schedules of 25, 15, and 5 fractions per course, and prespecified income-stratified Moderate and Ambitious hypofractionation pathways. Country-specific utilisation was examined as an access-constrained sensitivity scenario. Results: Across all scenarios, global EBRT-associated emissions increased from 2022 to 2050. With 25-fraction delivery, emissions rose from 43.02 to 67.94 MtCO2e under the 50% utilisation and from 55.06 to 86.96 MtCO2e under the 64% utilisation. Under the 50% benchmark, 15- and 5-fraction schedules reduced 2050 emissions to 40.76 and 13.59 MtCO2e, respectively. Emissions shifted towards middle-income settings: the high-income share declined from 42.9% to 36.5%, while the 10 countries with the largest modelled EBRT-associated emissions still accounted for 64.5% of global emissions in 2022 and 60.6% in 2050. Compared with a uniform 25-fraction baseline, the Moderate pathway reduced global emissions by 23.3% in 2022 and 21.9% in 2050, while the Ambitious pathway reduced emissions by 36.5% and 34.7%, respectively. The largest absolute reductions occurred in high-income and upper-middle-income settings. Conclusion: Global EBRT-associated emissions are projected to rise substantially by 2050. Clinically appropriate hypofractionation offers a high-leverage mitigation opportunity, with priorities differing between decarbonising established high-volume systems and embedding low-carbon delivery during capacity expansion.

items.title: Methylphenidate for Hematologic Cancer-Related Fatigue: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Frederiksen H, Gregersen H, Möller S, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Patients with hematologic cancer rate fatigue as their most frequent and severe unmet issue. Methylphenidate (MTP) has been reported to alleviate cancer-related fatigue (CRF) in some studies, but data from hematologic cancers are lacking. We investigated MTP for hematologic CRF. Methods: Using a double-blinded, placebo-controlled, two-period, crossover design, 152 adult fatigued patients with hematologic cancer were randomly assigned to 6 weeks of either MTP or placebo, with a treatment-free week before the crossover. Eligibility required a Visual Analog Scale fatigue score ≥4 (range, 0-10), hemoglobin ≥8.0 g/dL, no chemotherapy within 8 weeks, and no concomitant psychopharmacologic treatment. The primary end point was the between-group difference in the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) score from baseline to end of each period. Results: The median age was 59.0 years (range, 21-83), 44% were women, the performance status was 0 in 57.3%, and 11% had received high-dose therapy. FACIT-F improved 8.9 points (95% CIs, 7.3 to 10.4) after MTP and 3.9 points (95% CI, 2.3 to 5.4) after placebo. The between-group difference of 5.0 points (95% CI, 2.8 to 7.2) was in favor of MTP. Reduced fatigue ratings in favor of MTP were also observed using other tools. Toxicity was mild, but more adverse events were reported during the MTP (N = 73; 57%) versus placebo (N = 52; 40%) periods. Conclusion: MTP treatment alleviated fatigue and may be considered as a pharmacologic fatigue intervention in patients with hematologic cancer.

items.title: An uncertainty-aware deep learning-based registration model for adaptive lung cancer radiotherapy
items.authors: Wei C, Radonic D, Klaar R, et al.
items.abstract: To develop a deep learning (DL) based probabilistic 3D deformable image registration framework for uncertainty-aware dose accumulation in magnetic resonance imaging-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) of lung cancer.Approach: We propose TransMorph-prob (TM-prob), a variational Bayesian model that predicts the voxel-wise mean and variance of dense displacement fields (DDFs). Two TM-prob models were trained on an internal CT dataset (725 patients) and a low-field MR-linac dataset (102 patients), and benchmarked against Monte Carlo dropout TransMorph (TM-MCD) and DIRUncertainty with B-spline initialization (ASDIR) on the DIRLAB 4DCT dataset (10 patients, 3000 landmarks), and an annotated MR-linac dataset (16 patients, 107 image pairs, 227 landmarks) with target and seven organ-at-risk (OAR) contours. Both datasets contained an additional 1239/13,289 algorithm-generated landmarks. Performance was evaluated using target registration error (TRE), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), landmark- and voxel-wise expected calibration errors (LECE/ECE), and dose distributions derived from 2000 DDF samples per patient.Main results: On the DIRLAB dataset, TM-prob achieved a median TRE of \qty{1.8}{\mm}/\qty{2.8}{\mm} on manual/algorithm-generated landmarks, versus \qty{1.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.4}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{2.1}{\mm}/\qty{3.0}{\mm} for TM-MCD. On the MRI dataset, TM-prob achieved the median TRE of \qty{3.9}{\mm}/\qty{2.6}{\mm} and a mean DSC of 0.87, matching ASDIR (\qty{3.3}{\mm}/\qty{2.7}{\mm}, and DSC of 0.87) while outperforming TM-MCD (\qty{4.4}{\mm}/\qty{2.9}{\mm}, and 0.84). In uncertainty calibration, TM-prob achieved a LECE of \qty{1.74}{\mm}/\qty{0.30}{\mm} on MRI manual/algorithm-generated landmarks versus \qty{2.41}{\mm}/\qty{0.56}{\mm} for ASDIR and \qty{6.65}{\mm}/\qty{3.92}{\mm} for TM-MCD, and an average contour ECE of 5.8% versus 7.0% and 21.2%. Two patients with indistinct GTV boundaries exhibited substantially wider target D95 distributions, demonstrating that calibrated DDF uncertainty translates into clinically relevant dose-coverage uncertainty.Significance: TM-prob is an end-to-end DL model, achieving fast, well-calibrated, uncertainty-aware registration for lung cancer patients, enabling reliable DDF uncertainty propagation into dose accumulation for clinical decision-making in online adaptive radiotherapy.

items.title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning
items.authors: Touati R, Roberge D, Kadoury S
items.abstract: Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. Appraoch: We propose a radiotherapy planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT). The model combines a hybrid network with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation, with a refinement network. Main results: Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck, brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the Mean Absoluate Error (MAE) in Hounsfield units, as well as improved Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Gradient Magnitude Similarity Deviation (GMSD) compared to other DDPM and GAN approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best Mean Square Error (MSE) of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray in the head and neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a Conformity Index (CI) of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a Homogeneity Index (HI) of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance: Performance shows promise in integration for radiotherapy in head and neck, as well as in brain cancers.

items.title: Development of the Children's Oncology Group long-term follow-up guideline for cancer genetics evaluation in childhood cancer survivors
items.authors: Janardan SK, Devine A, Grieve LM, et al.
items.abstract: Up to 12% of childhood cancer survivors have an underlying cancer predisposition syndrome (CPS). As a result, these childhood cancer survivors are at increased risk for developing and succumbing to subsequent malignant neoplasms. Identifying childhood cancer survivors with CPS is essential to improving overall outcomes by informing tailored approaches to cancer screening, treatment, and, for some, risk-reducing interventions. Despite these potential benefits, it is often unclear which childhood cancer survivors warrant referral for genetic counselling and germline genetic testing. Using an evidence-based approach, a standardised guideline for referral for cancer genetics evaluation of childhood cancer survivors at high risk of having a CPS was developed and incorporated into the Children's Oncology Group Long-Term Follow-Up Guidelines for Survivors of Childhood, Adolescent, and Young Adult Cancers. This Policy Review details the importance, development, and anticipated impact of this new guideline. Raising awareness of this guideline is crucial to enhancing the integration of genetics into survivorship care and improving health outcomes for childhood cancer survivors with CPS.

items.title: Quantitative assessment of deformable image registration accuracy for cumulative dose estimation in multi-site stereotactic re-irradiation
items.authors: Yoosuf ABM, Aziz MZA, Alshehri S, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Re-irradiation of previously treated anatomical sites requires precise cumulative dose estimation to balance tumor control with organ-at-risk (OAR) tolerance. Conventional physical dose summation fails to account for inter-treatment anatomical deformations, potentially leading to systematic over- or underestimation of OAR doses. This study evaluates intensity-based deformable image registration (DIR) for improving dose accumulation accuracy in multiple stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) re-irradiation across different anatomical sites. Methods: Sixty patients (226 lesions) who underwent robotic CyberKnife-based SABR re-irradiation (2-5 courses) to liver (36.7%), brain (36.7%), lung (10%), and spine (16.7%) metastases between 2016 and 2025 were analyzed. Cumulative OAR doses were calculated using both DIR-based approach and traditional physical summation. DIR registration accuracy was quantified using dice similarity coefficient (DSC), jaccard index (JI). Biologically effective dose (BED) and equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2) conversions were evaluated for dose assessments across heterogeneous fractionation schedules. Results: DIR-based dose accumulation demonstrated significantly lower maximum doses compared with physical summation: liver maximum dose decreased from 123.8 ± 55.6 Gy to 83.2 ± 28.0 Gy (p < 0.001) and chest wall maximum dose reduced from 82.9 ± 22.4 Gy to 66.9 ± 18.6 Gy (p = 0.05). DIR yielded excellent spatial agreement for relatively rigid structures, including the heart, liver, kidneys, and brainstem (DSC > 0.90; JI > 0.84), whereas highly deformable organs such as the bowel and stomach demonstrated markedly inferior agreement (DSC < 0.50; JI < 0.35). Biological dose assessment revealed that DIR-guided workflow more accurately reflected cumulative dose patterns. Conclusion: Deformable registration improves cumulative dose estimation accuracy for multiple SABR re-irradiation. Integration of validated DIR with quantitative quality assurance and biological dose modeling provides a robust framework for multiple re-irradiation workflows. Future prospective studies correlating DIR-derived doses with clinical toxicity are warranted to validate the clinical impact of improved dosimetric accuracy.

items.title: Sequencing of Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy and Chemotherapy in Stage I Small Cell Lung Cancer: Practice Patterns and Outcomes
items.authors: Ziaks TJ, Oh P, Hicks D, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: We evaluated practice patterns and survival outcomes associated with the sequencing of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) and chemotherapy in patients with clinical stage I small cell lung cancer (SCLC) in the United States. Methods And Materials: Using a large national database, we identified patients with clinical stage I (cT1-2N0M0) SCLC treated with SBRT and chemotherapy between 2004 and 2020. To assess practice patterns in relation to survival outcomes, patients were categorized into 2 cohorts: "SBRT before chemotherapy" and "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy." χ2 tests and logistic regression models were used to determine patient characteristics associated with treatment sequencing. Univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazard models were used to assess the association between patient characteristics and survival outcomes. Overall survival was analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared via the log-rank test. Sensitivity analyses were performed using multivariable logistic regressions and Cox proportional hazards models for treatments with a 30-day overlap and clinical T stage stratification. Results: Among 631 patients with clinical stage I SCLC who were treated with SBRT and chemotherapy, 416 (65.9%) were categorized in "SBRT before chemotherapy" and 215 (34.1%) in "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy." Patients diagnosed after 2018 were less likely to receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy (odds ratio, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.32-0.66; P < .001). Patients diagnosed with clinical stage T2 were more likely to receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy (odds ratio, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.05-2.95; P = .03). No statistically significant difference in survival was observed between the 2 treatment sequencing cohorts ("SBRT before chemotherapy": median, 40.5 months vs "SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy": median, 35.6 months; log-rank P = .30). On multivariable analysis, SBRT sequencing was not associated with overall survival (hazard ratio = 1.11; P = .35; 95% CI, 0.89-1.37). Conclusions: Our findings suggest that there is no statistically significant difference in survival outcomes for patients who receive SBRT before chemotherapy compared with those who receive SBRT concurrent with or after chemotherapy. Therefore, flexibility in treatment sequencing may be appropriate in this population.

items.title: User Interface Designs to Address Cancer Misinformation: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Lazard AJ, Avendaño-Galdamez M, Queen TL, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Misinformation about false and potentially harmful cancer treatments is common on social media. Strategies are needed to encourage reporting to reduce exposure to inaccurate treatment claims. Objective: To evaluate the impact of 2 user interface designs (prompts on posts) on intervening and sharing cancer misinformation on social media. Design, Setting, And Participants: This 3-group, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial assessed outcomes at 5 time points from March 31 to May 12, 2025. US adults (ages 18-65 years) who had a cancer diagnosis or identified as a cancer caregiver and used social media were recruited from Prolific. Participants interacted with cancer misinformation posts on a simulated realistic social media platform. Data were analyzed from May 13, 2025, to July 27, 2026. Interventions: Participants were randomized to cancer misinformation posts shown with social cue-enhanced prompts that specify others' actions and a review policy, standard prompts, or no prompts (control). Main Outcomes And Measures: The primary outcome was a participant flagging a post to intervene. Primary and secondary outcomes included recorded social media behavior (flagging, disliking, liking) and self-reported willingness to flag, dislike, like, comment, and share about the posts. Intervening outside the study platform was also assessed. A separate generalized estimating equations model was used for each outcome. Results: A total of 294 individuals (mean [SD] age, 39.3 [11.7] years; 179 [62%] women) with cancer or who were caregivers for individuals with cancer were randomized, with 88 participants receiving social cue prompts, 92 receiving standard prompts, and 114 receiving no prompts. Posts with inaccurate claims were flagged 2 to 3 times more often with social cue (224 of 592 posts [38%]) and standard (180 of 689 posts [26%]) prompts than those without prompts (84 of 675 posts [12%]) (social cue vs control: rate ratio [RR], 3.12 [95% CI, 1.79-5.42]; standard vs control: RR, 2.15 [95% CI, 1.20-3.88]). Prompts led to less sharing behavior (ie, liking: 20 posts [3%] with social cue prompts; 10 posts [1%] with standard prompts) compared with posts without prompts (65 posts [10%]) (social cue vs control: RR, 0.07 [95% CI, 0.04-0.15]; standard vs control: RR, 0.13 [95% CI, 0.04-0.42]). items.authors: Manz CR, Tramontano AC, Voligny E, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Cancer is the leading cause of death in prison. Limited literature suggests cancer screening rates in prison are low, but population-level screening data in prisons are scarce. Objective: To determine screening rates for 5 cancer types, identify individual and incarceration characteristics associated with receipt of screening, and characterize outcomes for screen-detectable cancers in California prisons. Design, Setting, And Participants: This cohort study included individuals incarcerated in California state prisons who were eligible for breast, cervical, colorectal, liver, or lung cancer screening between January 1, 2014, and June 30, 2023. Incarceration data were linked to state cancer registry data from 2014 to 2021 to identify screen-detectable cancers diagnosed in the study population. Analyses were conducted between August 2024 and July 2025. Exposures: Receipt of screening within 3 months before a cancer diagnosis. Main Outcomes And Measures: Receipt of cancer screening; screening rates; and cancer diagnosis, stage, and survival were calculated. Multivariable models evaluated characteristics associated with screening receipt and associations between screening receipt and stage at diagnosis and survival, with adjustment for demographic and incarceration characteristics. Results: The study included 106 352 incarcerated individuals (median [IQR] age at first eligibility, 50 [47-55] years; 86 559 males [81.4%]). By June 30, 2023 (data cutoff), 89.4%, 81.2%, 80.0%, 70.1%, and 76.0% of individuals were up-to-date with screening for breast, colorectal, cervical, lung, and liver cancer screening, respectively. Characteristics associated with higher likelihood of ever receiving screening included mental health service use, prison security level 3 or 4, recent change in primary care practitioner, and incarceration within the past year before screening eligibility. Of 812 patients with screening data, 92 (11.3%) were diagnosed with screen-detectable cancer before they met eligibility for screening, including 56 with liver cancer. A total of 392 screening-eligible patients (48.3%) were diagnosed with screen-detectable cancer while in prison during the study period. items.title: Experimental validation of time-driven proton PBS FLASH delivery on a clinical proton therapy system
items.authors: Krzempek D, Gajewski J, Jabłoński H, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Clinical proton pencil beam scanning systems use dose-driven delivery, limiting operation at ultra-high dose rates required for FLASH radiotherapy. Time-driven spot delivery, controlled by irradiation time rather than monitor chamber feedback, may enable FLASH operation. We implemented a non-clinical time-driven FLASH strategy on a clinical proton PBS system and experimentally validated its performance. Materials And Methods: FLASH delivery was achieved by increasing beamline transmission through the energy-selection system and replacing dose-driven spot control with time-driven delivery in the Scanning Controller Diagnostic mode. Beam transmission was evaluated at gantry angle 0°. Depth-dose distributions, beam optics, scanning accuracy and uniform field generation were assessed for 228.4 MeV protons at gantry angles of 0°, 180° and 270°. Results: Opening the ESS divergence-limiting slits increased beamline transmission from 8% to 57%, resulting in approximately 273 nA at the isocentre (1.7 × 1012 protons s-1) and an estimated peak on-axis average dose rate of 2.0 × 103 Gy s-1. An 11 × 11 spot field delivered 25 Gy in approximately 0.6 s, corresponding to an average field dose rate of 42 Gy s-1, with up to 90 Gy s-1 measured at higher doses. Proton range and Bragg peak width remained unchanged. Spot position deviations were below 0.5 mm, and uniform 4 × 4 cm2 fields with <3% flatness were achieved. Conclusions: Time-driven delivery enables experimental proton PBS operation at UHDR while maintaining beam characteristics suitable for reproducible dosimetry and radiobiological studies, providing a practical and experimentally characterised platform for preclinical proton PBS FLASH research.

items.title: A pivotal Phase 2 study of derazantinib for previously-treated, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 aberrations: FIDES-01
items.authors: Borad MJ, Droz Dit Busset M, Javle MM, et al.
items.abstract: Background Aims: To evaluate safety and efficacy of FGFR1-3 kinase inhibitor derazantinib, in advanced intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) harboring FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements (FGFR2F), mutations (FGFR2M), or amplifications (FGFR2A), previously treated with chemotherapy. Approach Results: Open-label, non-controlled Phase 2 trial. Patients with advanced iCCA, ≥1 prior chemotherapy, and FGFR2F (Substudy 1) or FGFR2M/FGFRA (Substudy 2), received once-daily oral derazantinib 300 mg until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, consent withdrawal or investigator decision to stop. Efficacy was assessed by central radiology review using RECIST v1.1. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR; Substudy 1) and 3-month progression-free survival (PFS3; Substudy 2). Other endpoints were PFS, ORR (Substudy 2), disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DOR), and overall survival (OS). In Substudy 1, ORR and DCR were 22.3% (23/103 partial responses) and 75.7%, respectively; median (95% CI) PFS was 8.1 (5.5,8.3) months, DOR was 6.5 (4.6,9.2) months, and OS was 17.2 (12.5,22.4) months. In Substudy 2, PFS3 was 63% (27/43), ORR was 9.3% (3 partial, 1 complete response), DCR was 69.8%, and OS was 11.9 (8.4,15.9) months. There were no Grade 4 or 5 drug-related events. FGFR inhibitor class-specific toxicities included drug-related hyperphosphataemia (38%, Grade 3: 3%) and dry eye (36%). Nail disorders (10%, any grade or causality), stomatitis (5%), retinal events (5%), and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (1%) were infrequent. Conclusions: In previously chemotherapy treated, FGFR-inhibitor-naïve patients with iCCA harboring FGFR2 fusions, mutations, or amplifications, derazantinib showed clinically meaningful efficacy with durable objective responses, and a manageable safety profile.

items.title: Society of Surgical Oncology Best Practice Statement on the Implementation of New Programs and Technologies Into Practice: An IDEAL-Informed Framework
items.authors: Ocuin LM, Hwang RF, Park KU, et al.
items.abstract: Innovation in surgical oncology is developing rapidly, and new therapies and technologies have expanded across academic centers, integrated networks, and community sites, at times outpacing the evidence, expertise, and necessary infrastructure. Although innovation is essential to our field's progress, patient safety and demonstrated efficacy must remain paramount. Adopting specialized or understudied approaches without appropriate guardrails risks patient harm and generates low-quality, confusing evidence that impedes progress for future patients with cancer. To provide structured, practical guidance on this challenge to our field, the Society of Surgical Oncology Quality Committee recommends application of the IDEAL framework for surgical innovation, which organizes the life cycle of new procedures, programs, and technologies into five stages: idea (stage 1), development (stage 2a), exploration (stage 2b), assessment (stage 3), and long-term study (stage 4). Using expert consensus, we illustrate this IDEAL-informed approach with four examples that represent the breadth of the current implementation landscape in surgical oncology: hepatic artery infusion pump chemotherapy, robotic nipple-sparing mastectomy, histotripsy, and artificial intelligence. These technologies are used as concrete illustrations of principle, not as the primary subject of this statement. The central tenant is this: before any program or technology is broadly taken to the bedside, there must be evidence to support its efficacy. The recommendations described in this report have been endorsed by the Society of Surgical Oncology.

items.title: Experimental feasibility study of proton therapy range verification by a digital tracking calorimeter prototype
items.authors: Schilling A, Alme J, Barnaföldi GG, et al.
items.abstract: Objective.Uncertainties in the proton range remain an important challenge in proton therapy. In-situ range verification techniques can be used to ensure the Bragg peak depth in the patient matches the treatment plan. Various such methods are under investigation, utilizing the signal from secondary radiation caused by proton interactions with the patient. This study experimentally investigates the feasibility of using a silicon-pixel-based sampling calorimeter for range verification through the detection of secondary photons and neutrons.Approach.The proton range verification capability of a sampling calorimeter based on monolithic active pixel sensors was tested both theoretically and experimentally. We theoretically investigate the plausibility of the planned sampling calorimeter to pick up a signal from the neutral secondary particles distal to the patient. Then, a smaller prototype pixel telescope was constructed to verify our theoretical findings experimentally by placing it behind a water tank irradiated by a medical proton beam with various energies in the range of 100-200 MeV at the Danish Centre for Particle Therapy, Aarhus, Denmark.Main results.We find that the aluminum used as absorbers between sensitive layers in the calorimeter serves as a converter for prompt gammas and neutrons. The combined detection efficiency ranges between 5.8·10-5and 2.7·10-3detector hits per primary proton for beam energies between 50 and 200 MeV. Irradiation of the water phantom leads to a signal in our detector, which is well-correlated with the nominal beam energy. A simulation-based model using only the number of hits per proton can predict the beam energy, acting as a proxy for proton range in a homogeneous target, down to a root mean squared error of 1.34 MeV.Significance.This study marks a promising step towards utilizing a tracking calorimeter designed for proton computed tomography for the secondary application of proton therapy range verification without additional hardware costs.

items.title: Statewide surveillance of colorectal cancer screening using geospatial and Multi-Payer claims data
items.authors: Reeder-Hayes KE, Jackson BE, Lund J, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Screening is a key tool to improve colorectal cancer (CRC) outcomes and mitigate disparities, and reliable estimates of screening variation across communities can help prioritize screening interventions. However, existing screening surveillance infrastructure relies on labor-intensive telephone survey methodology. We aimed to develop novel methods of estimating CRC utilization for small geographic areas using North Carolina multi-payer claims data and to identify patterns and determinants of geographic variation in screening adherence. Methods: Using data from the Cancer Information and Population Health Resource, a multi-payer claims database, we generated annual screen-eligible cohorts and identified screening procedures. We then used Bayesian spatial models to estimate screening adherence for 1180 zip-code-based small areal units. We used geographic contextual data to re-weight estimates from the insured to the total (uninsured + insured) population. We examined associations between area-level racial composition and screening adherence stratified by age and sex. Results: Across all years, the observed proportion of person-years up-to-date among insured age-eligible adults statewide was 80.3%; among all age-eligible adults, 75.8% were estimated to be up-to-date. Model-estimated screening adherence in small areas ranged between 43.1% and 93.1%. Increasing Black racial composition was associated with lower screening adherence across all sexes and age strata. Older age and female sex were associated with higher screening adherence. Conclusions: Model-based estimation of CRC adherence from insurance claims and geographic data is feasible at scale and yields comprehensive estimates at small-area levels. There is wide variation in community-level screening adherence, with many areas falling below public health targets.

items.title: Efficacy of immediate radiotherapy versus salvage radiotherapy in patients with de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma responsive to chemoimmunotherapy
items.authors: Zhang QT, He JR, Guo HB, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Chemoimmunotherapy has become the standard first-line treatment for de novo metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (dmNPC). However, the role and optimal timing of locoregional radiotherapy in dmNPC in the chemoimmunotherapy era remain unclear. This study aims to evaluate whether salvage locoregional radiotherapy (SLRRT), deferred until locoregional progression in patients with well-controlled distant metastases, compromises survival compared with immediate locoregional radiotherapy (ILRRT) in responders to first-line chemoimmunotherapy. Patients And Methods: This retrospective cohort study included consecutive patients with dmNPC who achieved a complete or partial response after first-line platinum-based chemotherapy combined with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 therapy. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to adjust for baseline characteristics. Survival outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analyses and a multivariate Cox regression model. Results: A total of 439 patients were included, with a median follow-up of 35.0 months (interquartile range, 24.0-45.2). Of these, 331 patients were assigned to the ILRRT cohort and 108 to the SLRRT cohort. After IPTW adjustment, SLRRT was not associated with inferior OS compared with ILRRT [2-year OS, 97.4% versus 90.1%; hazard ratio (HR) 0.93, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.54-1.59, P = 0.78]. SLRRT was associated with worse locoregional control (HR 4.78, 95% CI 2.98-7.66, P < 0.001) but better distant control (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.95, P = 0.03). Radiotherapy-related adverse effects were substantially more frequent in the ILRRT cohort. Conclusions: Deferring SLRRT until locoregional progression did not compromise survival among responders to first-line chemoimmunotherapy. These findings support a response-adapted, de-escalated treatment strategy that may reduce treatment-related toxicities and improve quality of life without adversely affecting survival.

items.title: A regenerative stem cell phenotype marked by ANXA1 defines aggressive colorectal cancer biology
items.authors: Rotte-Wettig, H. S., Domingo, E., Valbuena, G., Nasreddin, N., Harkin, A., Iveson, T., Saunders, M. P., Oien, K. A., Maka, N., Pezzella, F., Campo, L., Browne, M., Glaire, M., Hay, J., Edwards, J., Sansom, O. J., Kelly, C., Tomlinson, I., Kerr, R., Kerr, D., TransSCOT consortium,, imCMS Consortium,, Leedham, S., Church, D. N., Braeutigam, K., Koelzer, V. H.
items.abstract: Background: LGR5 and ANXA1 are markers for specific intestinal stem cell states. LGR5+/ANXA1- crypt base columnar cells (CBCs) maintain homeostasis, whereas ANXA1+/LGR5- regenerative stem cells (RSCs) are present in fetal and repairing epithelium. Both states have been described in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet their clinical significance remains unclear. We aimed to determine how ANXA1 and LGR5 expression relates to molecular subtype, immune microenvironment and outcome in CRC. Methods: Dual-colour in situ hybridisation for ANXA1 and LGR5 was performed on tissue microarrays from 2163 patients in the randomised SCOT trial (ISRCTN59757862). AI-based digital pathology quantified marker-positive area by compartment and image based consensus molecular subtype (imCMS). Markers were related to clinicopathological, molecular and immune data, and to survival using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox analyses. Results: ANXA1 and LGR5 showed inverse enrichment among a diverse group of parameters. ANXA1 was highest in CMS1 and LGR5 in CMS2, with CMS3 and CMS4 being intermediate. ANXA1 dominance was associated with right-sidedness, mismatch repair deficiency, BRAF-V600E mutation, high stromal content, T4 stage, low stromal FoxP3 and high epithelial CD68 density. Combining both markers improved prognostic discrimination compared with either alone (cancer-specific survival p<0.001; recurrence-free interval p=0.004), with ANXA1 dominance remaining an independent predictor of recurrence after adjustment (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.08-1.90, p=0.014). Conclusion: Relative ANXA1 enrichment defines an aggressive, stroma-rich, macrophage-enriched CRC subgroup with poor prognosis.

items.title: Gaussian process regression of HDR prostate biopsy dose for improved modelling of localization-induced uncertainty
items.authors: Muscat M, Crook J, Jirasek A, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Biopsy‐level dose interpretation after high‐dose‐rate prostate brachytherapy is limited by localization uncertainty, and separate voxelwise Monte Carlo summaries do not explicitly account for the axial spatial correlation present along a biopsy core. Purpose To develop and internally evaluate a biopsy‐level Gaussian process regression framework for assigning along‐core high‐dose‐rate prostate brachytherapy dose under localization uncertainty, and to test whether explicit modelling of axial spatial correlation improves uncertainty characterization relative to voxelwise Monte Carlo summaries treated independently. Methods We analyzed 27 MR‐informed, transrectal‐ultrasound (TRUS)‐guided transperineal template biopsies from 15 patients treated with high‐dose‐rate prostate brachytherapy. For each biopsy voxel, Monte Carlo localization perturbations were propagated to generate dose summaries and voxel‐specific variances. Biopsy‐specific empirical semivariograms were fitted with candidate covariance kernels, and ordinary‐mean heteroscedastic Gaussian process posteriors were computed along each core. Internal evaluation included latent‐profile residual diagnostics, kernel‐sensitivity analysis, and blocked cross‐validation using contiguous held‐out axial segments scored on held‐out points only. Results For the selected baseline kernel, Matérn ν=1.5$\nu = 1.5$, the across‐biopsy median voxel‐averaged standard deviation was 6.91 Gy for the Monte Carlo summaries and 2.60 Gy for the latent GP posterior. The median within‐biopsy reduction was 59.1%, with a median shrinkage ratio of 2.45. Fitted length scales were heterogeneous across biopsies, with median ℓ̂b=15.35$\widehat{\ell }_b = 15.35$ mm, while nugget fractions were typically small. Cohort standardized residuals were near‐centered with conservative spread. In blocked cross‐validation, predictive performance on held‐out points remained favorable, with median root‐mean‐square error of 1.99 Gy, median mean absolute error of 1.58 Gy, and median negative log predictive density of 3.28. Among the tested kernels, held‐out predictive error favored Matérn ν=1.5$\nu = 1.5$. Conclusion Along‐core dose interpretation after localization uncertainty should use a spatially correlated model rather than separate voxelwise summaries alone. This Gaussian process framework provides a covariance‐informed posterior dose representation with held‐out internal validation and offers a practical basis for biopsy‐level probabilistic quality assurance and future dose‐response analyses.

items.title: Analysis on radiation protection of FLASH treatment in conventional proton therapy facilities
items.authors: Wang Y, Deng C, Gao N, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background FLASH radiotherapy is an advanced radiotherapy technique featuring ultra‐high dose‐rate irradiation. Previous preclinical studies have shown that it can significantly reduce damage to normal tissues while preserving the ability to kill tumor cells. Due to the very high current intensity of FLASH radiotherapy, the effectiveness of radiation shielding in current proton therapy facilities needs to be evaluated prior to clinical studies. Purpose Based on the existing shielding conditions of a ProBeam proton therapy system for conventional proton therapy treatment, we studied the shielding effectiveness of FLASH treatment in both the transmission and Bragg‐peak modes. Methods Under the conditions of single‐point irradiation using a proton beam with the highest clinical energy of 244MeV, and the beam intensity of 5nA, 10nA, and 20nA at the nozzle, the ambient equivalent dose rate outside the shielding door was measured with neutron and γ detector, in order to determine the linear relationship between the current intensity and the ambient dose rate. In addition, a gantry room was used as the study object, and the layout design of the points of interest was carried out according to the layout of the proton treatment facility and the transport path and direction of the proton beam, and the most unfavorable working conditions were set for each point of interest. The beam energy was set to 244 MeV, with a cylindrical water phantom (20 cm in diameter) and a solid water block (40 × 40 × 40 cm3) placed at the isocenter. The current at the nozzle was set to 20 nA, and comprehensive environmental dose rate measurements were carried out for the proton radiation workplace. Results A linear relationship was observed between nozzle current and ambient dose equivalent rate. Based on the linear relationship, when the current was extrapolated to a FLASH current of 170 nA, the measured instantaneous dose rates at some locations were relatively high, with the maximum value of 74.04 µSv/h recorded outside the shielding door. Under the conservative assumption that the total annual beam delivery time is 5 h (treating 6 patients per hour), the maximum annual occupational exposure doses for radiation workers under the transmission and Bragg Peak modes are 0.370 mSv and 0.236 mSv, respectively, which are well below the annual occupational dose limit.…

items.title: A generalizable 3D dose prediction across heterogeneous cohorts: A framework developed for the 2025 AAPM GDP-HMM challenge
items.authors: Abdulkadir Y, Neylon J, Lamb JM
items.abstract: Abstract Background Manual radiotherapy treatment planning is labor‐intensive, subjective, and highly variable across planners and institutions. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach for estimating achievable three‐dimensional (3D) dose distributions for a given plan (hereafter: dose prediction) by directly mapping patient anatomy and beam geometry to voxel‐wise dose. However, achieving robust generalization across diverse anatomical sites, prescriptions, and institutions remains a major challenge, particularly under computational constraints required for clinical deployment. Purpose We sought to develop and evaluate a generalizable, computationally efficient 3D dose prediction framework capable of spanning heterogeneous multi‐site and multi‐cohort datasets, as defined in the 2025 AAPM Generalizable Dose Prediction for Heterogeneous Multi‐Cohort and Multi‐Site (GDP‐HMM) Grand Challenge. Our goal was to design a model that not only achieved state‐of‐the‐art voxel‐wise accuracy but also maintained clinically meaningful dose‐volume and geometric characteristics across diverse cases. Methods We implemented a fully convolutional 3D dose‐prediction model adapted from the MedNeXt architecture, which was originally introduced as a high‐capacity convolutional backbone for medical image segmentation and is well suited to volumetric dense prediction tasks. The network accepted multimodal inputs comprising CT, PTV/OAR masks, beam and angle plates, and scalar plan metadata. A composite loss function combined voxel‐wise L1, body‐masked weighted L1, structure‐wise moment‐matching, and gradient‐based penalties to jointly preserve spatial fidelity and dosimetric accuracy. The model was trained on the fixed GDP‐HMM dataset consisting of 2876 training plans, 356 validation plans, and a held‐out test set of 498 plans using random 3D patches and evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE), homogeneity index (HI), and conformity indices (CI100%, CI50%). Ablation studies quantified the contribution of each loss component to overall performance. Statistical comparisons used paired Wilcoxon tests with false discovery rate correction. Results The proposed model achieved a mean voxel‐wise MAE of 2.04 Gy on the validation set, outperforming the challenge baseline (2.54 Gy). An ensemble with the baseline further improved MAE to 1.94 Gy on the validation set and 2.071 Gy on the held‐out test set, corresponding to the lowest test‐set MAE and first‐place overall ranking in the GDP‐HMM Challenge.…

items.title: Spot size reduction and minibeam creation in a proton PBS nozzle using multipole permanent magnets
items.authors: McAuley GA
items.abstract: Abstract Background Smaller spot sizes in pencil beam scanning (PBS) nozzles are generally desired to allow more conformal treatments and to spare normal tissue and organs at risk. The production of small diameter proton beams, especially proton minibeams, is challenging because long drift spaces in standard PBS nozzles exacerbate effects of MCS and finite beam divergence. Purpose To investigate the use of multipole magnets in a proton PBS nozzle to create pencil beams of reduced spot size, including the creation of proton minibeams. Methods Monte Carlo simulations were performed in a shortened He‐filled nozzle incorporating a doublet of octupole magnets and a single quadrupole magnet modeled as Halbach cylinders. Beam diameter reduction was realized by the combination of octupole tail folding and quadrupole magnetic focusing. The octupole doublet was positioned at nozzle entrance upstream of the scanning magnets and the quadrupole was (optionally) positioned at the nozzle exit. The nozzle was configured for four modes of operation, roughly described as standard pencil beam (PB mode), reduced‐diameter pencil beam (PBR), symmetric minibeam (MB), and planar minibeam (MBP). Depending on nozzle mode, symmetric beam spots were produced by a continuous rotation (i.e., spinning) of the octupole doublet and the quadrupole magnet about the beam axis. Particle energies investigated covered nearly the full range typically used in clinical applications (70, 100, 150, and 225 MeV). A symmetric Gaussian beam model was used with σ = 3 mm (FWHM = 7 mm) and σ’ (divergence) chosen from literature. Pencil beam and reduced diameter pencil beam dose distributions in a water phantom were compared. Minibeam composite dose distributions were created by laterally shifting single beamlet distributions in one or two dimensions, and PVDR and beamlet FWHM were determined. Modulated beams in each nozzle mode were also created. Results FWHM, FW20M, and penumbra were reduced for all PBR pencil beams compared to unshaped PB beams: at nozzle exit FWHM and FW20M were 19%–38% lower and penumbra P80/20 were 14%–59% lower, and at Bragg depth the differential full widths and penumbra were generally present; with full widths up to 21% smaller, and penumbras up to 15% smaller. The creation of single‐layer planar and symmetric minibeams in MBP and MB modes showed minimum beamlet FWHM near water phantom entrance (e.g., 10 mm WED) as low as 0.7–1.4 mm and <2 mm up to a range of 3–4.5 cm of the entrance channel.…

items.abstract: The combination of lenvatinib and pembrolizumab has demonstrated efficacy in advanced renal cell carcinoma, as shown in the CLEAR study. And this therapy was approved in Japan on February 2022. However, data from real-world clinical practice in Japan remain limited.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: P114-3 JAVEMACS chart review of avelumab maintenance in advanced urothelial carcinoma in Japan: analysis in older patients
items.authors: K. Yonemori, H. Kitamura, H. Kimura, S. Shirotake, M. Ikeda, N. Kwawamura, T. Abe, K. Fujita, N. Hayakawa, H. Miyake, N. Miura, T. Negishi, J. Yatusda, N. Nishiyama, R. Taoka, M. Kobayasshi, J. Furukawa, M. Syouno, T. Kobayashi, E. Kikuti
items.abstract: Avelumab maintenance therapy is approved for patients (pts) with curatively unresectable urothelial carcinoma (UC) not progressed after first-line (1L) platinum-based chemotherapy (PBC). The increasing proportion of pts aged ≥75 years (y) with UC, who are often underrepresented in clinical trials, underscores the need to assess their treatment outcomes in clinical practice. Here we report long term efficacy analyses data for older subgroups from JAVEMACS chart review study of avelumab maintenance therapy in Japan.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: P098-11 Assessing efficacy and safety of pembrolizumab combined with chemoradiation in NSCLC: a systematic review
items.authors: J.K. Susanto, M.A. Chan, N. July, J.A. Susanto, I.L. Donsinghani, J.A.S. Kho, A. Kurniawan
items.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for 85% of lung cancers, despite slower progression than small cell lung cancer, is often diagnosed at advanced stages with poor prognosis. Pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, enhances immune-mediated tumor control, while chemoradiation remains the standard for locally advanced disease by combining systemic cytotoxicity with local tumor control. Their combination represents a rational therapeutic strategy.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: P056-8 Initial experience with the watch & wait strategy for localised rectal cancer in a regional hospital in Mallorca, Spain
items.authors: A. M. Merce Pascual, N. M. Mesquida Luque, I. C. Cutillas Cerda, C. S. Sanchez Pardo, T. F. Fernandez Rodriguez
items.abstract: The Watch and Wait (W&W) strategy after a complete clinical response (cCR) in rectal cancer has consolidated as an alternative in the organ preservation approach. In Spain, the first pilot experience started years earlier, but it was not until 2022 that it was introduced in our hospital, and until April 2024 that the first Spanish consensus was published. Still, data from smaller centers remains limited.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: P031-9 Efficacy and safety of gemcitabine plus cisplatin for nasopharyngeal carcinoma: a retrospective analysis of five cases
items.authors: M. Nakamoto, H. Takahashi, A. Yoshiba, M. Sakuramachi, H. Igaki, M. Itoyama, R. Morita, H. Imazeki, S. Yamamoto, K. Kato, Y. Honma
items.abstract: Gemcitabine plus cisplatin (GC) is recommended as a preferred regimen for advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) in international guidelines, including the NCCN (v.2025) and CSCO/ASCO guidelines, either as induction or palliative chemotherapy. However, GC has not been approved for NPC in Japan, and clinical data on its efficacy and safety in Japanese patients remain limited.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: P017-2 Proton beam therapy vs radiotherapy in pediatric medulloblastoma: a systematic review of survival and cognitive outcomes
items.authors: R. Dharmawan, K. Ivanna, H. Aysha, I. Akim, A. Kurniawan
items.abstract: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, accounts for 20% of pediatric Central Nervous System tumors. Conventional radiotherapy (RT) improves survival but often causes neurocognitive decline, endocrine dysfunction and secondary cancers. Proton beam therapy (PBT) may offer similar tumor control with reduced toxicity.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: P003-8 Real-world efficacy and safety of CPX-351 in high-risk acute myeloid leukemia
items.authors: R. Saito, S. Kikuchi, S. Fujimoto, A. Shichishima-Nakamura, H. Noji, S. Saji
items.abstract: CPX-351 (Vyxeos®) is a liposomal formulation encapsulating daunorubicin and cytarabine at a fixed 1:5 molar ratio. Maintaining this ratio stabilizes pharmacokinetics and enables selective delivery to leukemic blasts, improving efficacy. It is approved in Japan for high-risk acute myeloid leukemia (AML), including therapy-related and secondary AML, populations with poor outcomes under conventional chemotherapy. Real-world evidence in Japanese clinical practice remains limited.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: MO17-2 Outcomes of CDK4/6 inhibitor switching in HR+/HER2- advanced breast cancer at Ho Chi Minh City Oncology Hospital
items.authors: T. Nguyen Nhu, D. Phan Thi Hong, T. Diep Bao, H. Vo Duc, P. Vo Hong Minh, Q. Nguyen Hoang, T. Phan Tan, H. Vo Ngoc, T. Nguyen Thi Thuy
items.abstract: Endocrine therapy combined with cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) is the current standard of care for patients with hormone receptor-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HR+/HER2-) advanced breast cancer. In Vietnam, ribociclib and palbociclib have been available since March 2021. In clinical practice, some patients develop early intolerance or adverse events. International studies suggest that switching to another CDK4/6i due to toxicity may preserve efficacy.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: MO07-1 Transforming neoadjuvant therapy in gallbladder cancer: a prospective comparison of NACRT versus standard chemotherapy
items.authors: D. Khosla, T. Dey, R. Kapoor, R. Gupta, M. Kumar, S.S. Rana, H. Singh, J. Shah
items.abstract: Gallbladder carcinoma is a rare, aggressive cancer often diagnosed late. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) helps downstage disease, while neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NACRT) may improve locoregional control. This study evaluates feasibility and safety of NACRT in locally advanced cases, comparing outcomes with a parallel NACT-treated group outside the trial.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: MO04-2 Vitamin K supplementation preserves hip BMD in prostate cancer patients on ADT: a randomised double-blind clinical trial
items.authors: V. Prajapati, V. Kumar Verma, J. Bhatia, S. Kumar, A. Seth, D. Singh Arya
items.abstract: Prostate cancer is the second most common and sixth leading cause of cancer deaths in men worldwide. Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the mainstay in prostate cancer management. Amongst all the side effects of ADT, osteoporosis and bone fractures are of particular concern. Vitamin K regulates bone metabolism by acting as a cofactor in the carboxylation of osteocalcin in the bone matrix. Therefore, vitamin K plays a role in maintaining bone health. ADT induces vitamin K loss by an unknown mechanism and leads to osteoporosis and an increased risk of fractures.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: MO03-5 Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy plus surgery improves survival in locally advanced esophageal cancer: a meta analysis
items.authors: H.M. Gunawan, S. Budiman, J.E. Gunawan, A.I. Chandra
items.abstract: Esophageal carcinoma has poor prognosis, and surgery alone often results in high recurrence rates. Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy may improve tumor control and survival, but its benefit over surgery alone remains under evaluation.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: MO02-5 Efficacy and safety of adjuvant nivolumab in resected esophageal cancer after neoadjuvant chemoradiation
items.authors: R.F. Zein, C.C. Hermawan, E.N. Hailianto, T.C.E. Adeodatia
items.abstract: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery is standard for resectable esophageal cancer, yet recurrence remains high and no standard adjuvant therapy exists. Nivolumab, an immune checkpoint inhibitor, has emerged as a promising option. This review evaluates the efficacy and safety of adjuvant nivolumab in this high-risk population.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: MO02-1 Clinical outcomes of definitive chemoradiotherapy for esophageal cancer in the immune checkpoint inhibitor era
items.authors: S. Ishikawa, M. Furuta, Y. Mikuriya, M. Onishi, T. Hama, N. Minakata, K. Shiotsuki, H. Nakanoma, K. Takizawa, D. Yoshida, J. Furuse, S. Maeda
items.abstract: Definitive chemoradiotherapy (dCRT) is one of the standard treatments for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). However, most of the evidence originates from clinical trials conducted over two decades ago, which may not reflect recent advances in radiotherapy or the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) since 2020. This study aimed to clarify the outcomes of dCRT for ESCC in the modern era.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: MO01-5 Neoadjuvant adebrelimab + SOX + Nab-Pac in resectable LA-G/GEJ adenocarcinoma: preliminary data from a phase II trial
items.authors: J. Zhang, H. Duan, L. Cao, C. Zhang, Y. Li, P. Liang
items.abstract: We report preliminary results from an ongoing single-arm phase II clinical trial evaluating neoadjuvant adebrelimab combined with chemotherapy in patients with resectable locally advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction (LA-G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: SY28-1 Treatment advance and further perspectives in LD-SCLC
items.authors: N. Reinmuth
items.abstract: Achieving long-term survival has been only an exceptional event in patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Unfortunately, this also applies for patients with stage I-III SCLC after treatment with combined chemoradiotherapy. In fact, median progression-free survival of patients after combined chemoradiotherapy has been reported to be only 9.2 months despite the curative intent of the respective treatment.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: SY8 Can MRD serve as a surrogate endpoint in solid tumors?
items.authors: S. Nomura
items.abstract: Recent clinical research across multiple solid tumors has demonstrated a remarkably good prognostic stratification with the use of molecular residual disease (MRD). For patient populations with extremely favorable prognoses like in peri-operative settings, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) based on established endpoints such as disease-free survival, event-free survival, or overall survival often require infeasibly large sample sizes and prohibitively long follow-up. Interim assessments using MRD-related endpoints may offer a practical path to accelerate access of patients to effective therapies.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: PSY8-5 Advances in gastric cancer systemic therapy: current guidelines and clinical trial development in Taiwan
items.authors: M. Chen
items.abstract: Systemic therapy for gastric cancer in Taiwan has progressed substantially with the integration of molecular profiling, immunotherapy, and multidisciplinary care. National treatment guidelines have been updated in parallel with international evidence while reflecting clinical characteristics of East Asian patients, including higher disease burden and distinct biomarker distributions.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: PSY8-1 Asia's contributions to upper GI cancer care-from development to real-world implementation (keynote overview)
items.authors: K. Muro
items.abstract: This keynote lecture aims to clarify the role Asia has played in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (GC), and to discuss future challenges. Japan and Korea have established screening system that normalizes early detection in GC; consequently, many surgical cases are early disease. High procedural quality-routine EMR/ESD for T1 lesions and meticulous gastrectomy with adequate (often D2) lymphadenectomy-underpins favorable perioperative and long-term outcomes versus many Western countries.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: PSY2-2 Lung cancer research and practice in Taiwan
items.authors: J. Yang
items.abstract: Lung cancer management in Taiwan, similar to other types of cancer, is characterized by a centralized, hospital-based oncology practice. Diagnosis and treatment is concentrated in close to 70 accredited hospitals where multidisciplinary teams (MDTs) integrate thoracic surgeons, medical oncologists, and pulmonologists, radiation oncologists etc. The National Health Insurance (NHI), a single-payer system providing universal coverage. The practices follow world standard and most hospitals adopt NCCN guidelines.
source_names: Annals of Oncology

items.title: The evolving role of perioperative systemic therapy in bladder cancer
items.authors: Atiq SO, Anker JF, Miller EJ, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract The treatment landscape for muscle‐invasive bladder cancer has recently been transformed by two key phase 3 studies of perioperative enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab. These trials have demonstrated significant improvements in event‐free survival and overall survival compared with the previous standards of care, marking a new era in the management of patients with muscle‐invasive bladder cancer that is no longer defined by cisplatin eligibility. The focus is now shifting toward the identification of additional novel therapeutic targets for further improved outcomes as well as response‐guided treatment pathways seeking to optimize both cancer control and survivorship.

items.title: Association of HPV Status With Quality of Life After Transoral Robotic Surgery for T1-T2 Oropharyngeal Carcinoma
items.authors: Tesauro P, Khalaf M, Breuskin I, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background In T1–T2 oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), factors associated with patient‐reported quality of life after transoral robotic surgery (TORS) are poorly defined. Methods Retrospective cohort of 59 patients with T1–T2 OPSCC treated with TORS. Swallowing‐related quality of life (MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory, MDADI) and EORTC QLQ‐C30/QLQ‐H&N35 scores were analyzed with mixed‐effects models adjusted for HPV status, subsite, adjuvant treatment and, in sensitivity analyses, lifestyle factors, age, tumor stage, and preoperative scores. Results HPV‐positive status was independently associated with higher MDADI scores (β = 12.39, p = 0.001), including after adjustment for preoperative scores (β = 16.0, p = 0.004), and with lower QLQ‐H&N35 symptom burden (β = −9.5, p = 0.012). Adjuvant radiotherapy was associated with lower MDADI scores (β = −7.92, p = 0.021), attenuated after adjustment for tumor stage. Tumor subsite was not associated with outcomes. Conclusions HPV‐positive patients report better swallowing‐related quality of life after TORS, independently of preoperative scores.

items.title: A multicenter end-to-end postal audit of skin markerless surface-guided radiation therapy
items.authors: Saito M, Yamauchi R, Kojima H, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Surface-guided radiation therapy (SGRT) enables skin markerless positioning, but its accuracy may depend on the reference surface, hardware configuration, commissioning, and institutional workflow. Two reference surfaces are commonly used: a DICOM reference generated from planning CT images and an SGRT reference acquired in the treatment room. Multicenter end-to-end data across commercial systems remain limited. Purpose: To evaluate static irradiation accuracy and setup time with two reference surfaces in a nationwide multicenter skin markerless SGRT postal audit. Methods: A prospective end-to-end postal audit was conducted from October 2023 to July 2025 at 40 Japanese institutions using five commercial SGRT systems (AlignRT, Catalyst, ExacTrac Dynamic, IDENTIFY, and VOXELAN), eight per system. Each institution received a common phantom package: a breast-shaped surface phantom, two cubic phantoms containing gold markers, and radiochromic films. Markerless setup and irradiation were performed with both the DICOM and SGRT references; ExacTrac Dynamic institutions performed the DICOM reference setup only. Static irradiation accuracy was the difference between the film-derived radiation center and the intended center in the DICOM RT Plan; the primary metric was the three-dimensional translational vector error (3D vector error). Paired comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and multivariable linear regression evaluated factors associated with both endpoints. Results: Critical setup errors exceeding 5 mm occurred at four institutions initially (institution-level error rate, 10.0%; three with the DICOM and one with the SGRT reference); one DICOM reference setup was not remeasured and remained out of tolerance, and was excluded as an outlier, leaving 39 DICOM and 31 SGRT reference setups for analysis. Excluding ExacTrac Dynamic, the DICOM reference showed a significantly larger 3D vector error than the SGRT reference (1.54 ± 0.91 vs. 1.20 ± 0.61 mm, p = 0.043). Setup time did not differ between references (86.19 ± 43.57 vs. 81.61 ± 37.09 s, p = 0.804). Axis-specifically, the difference between references was confined to the anterior-posterior direction (mean absolute difference 0.36 mm, p = 0.002), whereas a caudal superior-inferior offset was present with both (-0.50 ± 1.29 and -0.37 ± 0.87 mm; both p < 0.01) and did not differ between them (p = 0.854).…

items.title: Technical development and implementation of 3D-QALAS on a 1.5T MR-Linac for the brain: A prospective R-IDEAL stage 0/1 technology development report
items.authors: McCullum L, Harrington A, West N, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Quantitative relaxometry of the brain on the integrated MRI / linear accelerator (MR-Linac) at high isotropic reconstructed resolution is currently limited due to prohibitively long scan times and limited field-of-views. Purpose: The purpose of this study was to assess the technical feasibility of the 3D-QALAS technique on the 1.5T MR-Linac which can acquire whole-brain 1 mm isotropic quantitative T1, T2, and PD maps along with multiple synthetic images in a 7-minute acquisition time. Methods: A 1 mm isotropic 3D-QALAS acquisition was scanned in both phantoms and five healthy volunteers on the 1.5T Elekta Unity MR-Linac device with scan times around seven minutes. A test-retest protocol across five independent sessions for the phantom was conducted. The Lin's Concordance Correlation Coefficient (LCCC), repeatability, and reproducibility between measured and reference quantitative T1, T2, and PD values were determined in the phantom. Distortion was also studied. Vendor-provided reconstruction through SyMRI was performed to extract synthetic images and brain volume metric assessments in the healthy volunteers. Results: The slope and LCCC between the measured and phantom reference values was 1.02 (1.00), 1.09 (0.90), and 0.99 (1.00) for T1, T2, and PD, respectively. Median distortion across the phantom remained below 2 mm. The repeatability and reproducibility coefficient-of-variation (CoV) was under 8% for all measured values. The measured brain volumes in the healthy volunteer was within expected age-adjusted reference values. Conclusions: The technical feasibility of using 3D-QALAS on the integrated 1.5T MR-Linac was confirmed. Applying this technique to the adaptive radiation therapy workflow of the brain will provide new opportunities to integrate quantitative imaging relaxometry biomarkers at 1 mm isotropic reconstructed resolution.

items.title: Physics-informed depth-enhanced surface tracking for cumulative dose reconstruction in breast radiotherapy: An in silico feasibility study
items.authors: Tang X, Qiu M, Deng Y
items.abstract: Purpose: Surface guided radiotherapy (SGRT) provides nonionizing motion monitoring but lacks direct correlation with internal dosimetric changes. Purely data-driven models for surface-to-internal deformation prediction often yield biomechanically implausible results. This study proposes a physics-informed depth-enhanced (PIDE) framework, validated in silico, to reconstruct internal deformation and cumulative dose from noisy surface measurements. Methods: A virtual clinical trial (VCT) was conducted using weekly cone-beam CT (CBCT) data from 29 breast cancer patients. We simulated consumer-grade RGB-D sensor noise ( σ ∝ z 2   ) on extracted patient surfaces. To map external surface features to internal deformation vector fields (DVF), we developed a regularized ridge regression model. Unlike traditional models, ours integrates a spectral energy penalty derived from patient-specific CBCT motion priors, constraining predictions to physically plausible deformations. Patient-specific clinical RTDOSE distributions and 348 anatomical landmarks were utilized to evaluate the dosimetric and geometric accuracy. Vector field smoothness was quantified using the Jacobian determinant. Results: Under realistic simulated sensor noise, the PIDE framework achieved an anatomical target registration error (TRE) of 1.33 ± 1.42 mm (compared to an initial misalignment of 2.14 ± 2.38 mm, representing a 37.8% error reduction). The physics-constrained regression yielded an RMSE of 2.31 mm (r = 0.720) for motion prediction and effectively eliminated nonphysical tissue "folding" artifacts (reducing negative Jacobian voxels from 0.54% to 0.10%, p = 0.0209). Dosimetric evaluation using actual patient treatment plans achieved a mean Gamma passing rate (3%/3 mm) of 99.68 ± 0.30% (range: 99.00%-100.00%), with 100% of patients (29/29) exceeding the 90% clinical safety threshold. The end-to-end algorithmic inference latency was 2.71 ms per frame, demonstrating high computational efficiency. Conclusion: The integration of geometric surface features with patient-specific physical constraints successfully prevents nonphysiological deformation artifacts caused by sensor noise. This in silico study demonstrates the feasibility and computational efficiency of the PIDE framework for rapid cumulative dose monitoring.

items.title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Trial
items.authors: Cachia JYA, Zhao X, Hunter J, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Young adults today face unprecedented mental health challenges, yet many hesitate to seek support owing to barriers such as accessibility, stigma, and time constraints. Bite-sized well-being interventions offer a promising solution to preventing mental distress before it escalates to clinical levels, but have not yet been delivered through personalized, interactive, and scalable technology. Methods: We conducted the first multi-institutional, longitudinal, preregistered randomized controlled trial of a generative artificial intelligence (AI)-powered mobile app (Flourish) designed to address this gap. Over 6 weeks in the fall of 2024, 486 undergraduate students from three U.S. institutions were randomly assigned to receive app access or to a care-as-usual control condition. Results: Participants instructed to use the Flourish app twice per week reported significantly greater resilience and social well-being (i.e., increased belonging, closeness to community, and reduced loneliness), and they were buffered against declines in positive affect, mindfulness, and flourishing. No significant condition-by-time effects were observed for depression, anxiety, or stress in this study with a general population. Conclusions: These findings suggest that, with purposeful and ethical design, generative AI can deliver proactive population-level well-being interventions that produce measurable benefits.

items.title: Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy Increases Genomic Radioresistance in Hormone Receptor-positive, Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2-Negative Breast Cancer: Implications for Radiation Sensitivity Index/Genomic-Adjusted Radiation Dose-Guided Radiation Therapy Personalization
items.authors: Loap P, Crehange G, Kirova Y
items.abstract: Purpose: Adjuvant radiation therapy (RT) improves locoregional control after breast cancer surgery, but dose prescription remains based mainly on clinicopathologic risk rather than individual tumor radiosensitivity. The radiation sensitivity index (RSI) and genomic-adjusted radiation dose (GARD) provide a framework for biologically guided radiation therapy personalization. In the neoadjuvant setting, however, radiosensitivity measured on the diagnostic biopsy may not reflect the residual disease ultimately targeted by adjuvant radiation therapy. Methods And Materials: We analyzed matched pretreatment and posttreatment RNA sequencing data from 2 public cohorts of hormone receptor-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HR+/HER2-) breast cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. The discovery cohort included 16 matched pairs from GSE191127, and the validation cohort included 14 matched HR+/HER2- pairs from GSE309004. The RSI was computed using a 10-gene rank-based model. The ΔRSI was defined as RSI_post - RSI_pre. Immune fractions were inferred using quanTIseq, and the GARD was calculated for START B, RTOG 1005, and FAST-Forward adjuvant radiation therapy schedules. Results: In the discovery cohort, the mean RSI increased from 0.602 to 0.677 after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, with 12 of 16 patients (75%) showing a posttreatment increase. In the validation cohort, the mean RSI increased from 0.489 to 0.593 (Wilcoxon P = .014), with 11 of 14 patients (78.6%) showing an increase. In the pooled cohort, the mean ΔRSI was +0.089, and 23 of 30 patients (76.7%) showed an increased RSI after chemotherapy (Wilcoxon P = .005). Higher pretreatment M2 macrophage fraction correlated with a larger ΔRSI. The RSI changes translated into heterogeneous GARD dose modifications across fractionation schedules. Conclusions: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is associated with a reproducible increase in RSI in HR+/HER2- breast cancer, suggesting that residual tumors may become more radioresistant at the genomic level after systemic therapy. A postneoadjuvant chemotherapy RSI warrants prospective evaluation for individualized adjuvant radiation therapy strategies.

items.title: Rapid Response Palliative Radiation Therapy Program: Feasibility and Experience of Implementing a Nonclassical Model
items.authors: Vargas A, Rivas H, Solé S
items.abstract: Purpose: Classical rapid access palliative radiation therapy (RAPRT) programs are typically organized as dedicated clinics designed to enable same-day consultation, simulation, treatment planning, and delivery of palliative radiation therapy. At our institution, urgent and expedited palliative radiation therapy is delivered through an integrated, nonclassical RAPRT model embedded in routine departmental practice. This study describes the implementation and performance of this model. Methods And Materials: We retrospectively reviewed patients treated by our RAPRT workflow between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2024. Demographic, clinical, treatment-related, and workflow data were collected from the institutional oncology information system and clinical records. Workflow intervals were calculated using electronic timestamps. Results: A total of 775 patients received 848 treatment courses; 37% were hospitalized at the time of treatment. Fifty-six patients (7.2%) received >1 treatment course, and 15 required reirradiation. The median time from referral to radiation oncology consultation was 1 day (Q1, 1; Q3, 3). Median age was 63 years (Q1, 54; Q3, 73), and the most common primary tumors were lung (25%) and gastrointestinal cancers (17%). Poor performance status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 3-4) was observed in 40% of cases. The most common treatment sites were bone (47%) and thorax (19%). A single fraction was prescribed in 797 extracranial courses, representing 94% of all courses. Median total treatment process time was 109 minutes (Q1, 102; Q3, 165), and median time spent in the radiation therapy center was 207 minutes (Q1, 111; Q3, 250). Time to simulation and dosimetry time were the most time-consuming workflow steps, accounting for 24% and 31% of the total workflow duration, respectively. Conclusions: An integrated, nonclassical RAPRT model using existing departmental resources is feasible and can achieve rapid palliative radiation therapy timelines comparable to those reported by dedicated RAPRT programs. Robust information systems and coordinated electronic workflows are central to the efficient implementation of this model.
